en: The *Vajra-Needle: Record for Revealing the Nature*, Volume One, compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān.
The *Vajra-Needle* is a treatise composed by the Great Master of Jīngqí based upon the Perfect and Sudden Teachings; it elucidates the intent of the Buddha.

This work, intended to expound the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), harmonizes the myriad phenomena within the single mind and silences divergent arguments for a thousand ages. Furthermore, it opens the eye of wisdom for future generations;
using the "Golden Scalpel" as its metaphorical title, it addresses the provisional doubts of previous eras by posing questions through the voice of a rustic guest.
Its Way is most vast and its noble words are profoundly manifest, ensuring that Buddha-nature shines brightly and is not obscured by deluded sentiments.
The recluse Yuan has cherished and contemplated this treatise for many years. Thereupon, he has selected from various sayings to expound its essential meaning;

his aim is self-illumination rather than to bestow it upon others. Having recorded the essential texts of our own school to manifest this wondrous principle of Buddha-nature, he has therefore titled it the *Xianxing lu* (Record of Manifesting Nature).
It was the third year of the Jingde era of the Huang Song dynasty.
Next is the preface for the autumn full moon day of the Bingwu year.
This treatise was composed precisely because worldly people cling to provisional texts regarding *nirvāṇa* and claim that tiles and stones lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, Jingxi, moved by a heart of compassion and pitying such inverted delusions, relied upon the "Inconceivable Realm" as elucidated in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) concerning the momentary mind (*kṣaṇika-citta*).

Within this [treatise], the three thousand dharmas—including the defiled and the pure, the environment and its inhabitants, cause and effect, and self and other—are fully encompassed without exception.
Since these are pervasive in every moment, the Buddha-nature consequently becomes all-encompassing; thus, one realizes that even tiles and stones are nothing but my own mind-nature.

Such is the intent behind the composition of this treatise. Now, following the general precedent of various sutras and looking up to our Patriarchs, I shall briefly set forth five meanings to explain the title of the first section, "General Overview."
To demonstrate the five meanings, they are presented individually following the general demonstration.
The five are: first, indicating the names; second, the origination; third, the common and specific applications; fourth, citing evidence; and fifth, resolving doubts.
Regarding the indication of the names: first, "analogy" as the name; second, "Buddha-nature" as the essence; third, "contemplative practice" as the primary tenet; and fourth, "dispelling delusion."
Regarding the employment of the five kinds of *amṛta* (clarified butter) as the teaching for the two types of birth:

since one who intends to discourse upon the ultimate principle must first rectify terminology, the merit of the Great Teaching is manifested by establishing the title "Golden Needle. Therefore, the name is explained first;

for by hearing the name, one recognizes the essence, just as one forgets the trap after catching the fish, so that one does not remain stuck to the metaphorical name but reaches the principle of Buddha-nature. Thus, the essence is explained next. Although...
The substance of the Buddha-nature has been clarified and its perfect fusion fully revealed; yet, without the school of wondrous practice, there would be no way to achieve realization.

Therefore, next, the "School" (zong) is clarified as self-cultivation, while the "Function" (yong) is clarified as transforming others. Since self-cultivation is established internally, external function then manifests. Thus, next, the "Function" is clarified through four meanings as a guiding compass.
Furthermore, one must distinguish between the various aspects of the teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*); otherwise, they would be indistinguishable like salt water and river water.

Water cannot distinguish between the hides of tigers and leopards; who can discern the differences between the square and the round without confusion? It is by classifying according to their respective categories that they are subsequently distinguished.

Thus, the subsequent clarification of the "characteristics of the teachings" (jiaoxiang) involves three aspects: the general, the specific, and the distinction between them. Regarding the various patriarchs of India and the teachers of China, each has expounded upon the Buddhist scriptures and composed various treatises.

If one understands the five chapters of the titles, the general meaning is clear; yet, as for the different schools of interpretation and the distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, these vary.

If one understands the five chapters of the title, they are distinguished by four citations of scriptural evidence. First, regarding the name: the text states that the "Golden Needle of the Perfect *E* (I)" is used to resolve the cataracts of ignorance of the four eyes;

thus, it takes "metaphor" as its name. Second, regarding the essence: the text states that we now establish the substance of the *samyak-hetu* (correct cause) of sentient beings as being all-pervasive, and the scripture also uses "empty space" as a metaphor for this;
thus, it takes "Buddha-nature" as its essence. Third, regarding the nature: the text states, "It is thus... [and so forth].

Contemplating this in reliance upon it, it is further stated that this is the Dharma transmitted by the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation); therefore, taking contemplative practice as its primary principle, the text says:

"If one contemplates a single question, all various obstructions will naturally dissolve. Furthermore, it states that the second [principle] reveals the inherent nature to cause one to reform their delusion;

thus, taking the destruction of delusion as its function, the text says: "Searching through the present and the future, one establishes the perfect fusion" (the "present" refers to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the "future" refers to...).

Furthermore, it is said that the wondrous realm (nirvāṇa) pointed out originates from the *Lotus Sūtra*; therefore, the "cream of cream" (*tīmadhu*) is employed as the characteristic of the teaching. Fifth, resolving doubts:
some may say, "The treatise (*śāstra*) generally follows the sūtra, yet while the sūtra establishes five meanings, these are not heard of in the treatise.

Now, we say this is not so. There are two kinds of treatises: first, those of independent tenets (*siddhānta-śāstra*), and second, commentaries (*vyākhyāna-śāstra*). If a commentary shares the same name as the sūtra...
If the meaning has no divergent interpretations, then the five meanings are merely set forth in various treatises (*zonglun*), their names differing from those in the sutras;
if the meaning does have divergent interpretations, then the five chapters are put to practical use. This *Vajrasamādhi* [Treatise] is precisely such a treatise.

Second, the specific exposition of the five meanings. First, regarding the explanation of the title, this is further divided into two parts: first, a combined explanation; second, a separate explanation. Regarding the combined explanation:
now, every treatise establishes its title for a specific reason. This present treatise establishes its title based on the analogy of the "Golden Scalpel" (*Suvarṇasūci*) from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Thus, as stated in the "Tathāgata-gotra" chapter: "For example, there were one hundred blind men who sought treatment for their eyes."
Therefore, he goes to a skilled physician. At that time, the physician uses a golden probe to cut away his cataracts and points with one finger, asking, "Do you see?
The blind man replies, "I still do not see. He then points with two fingers and three fingers, whereupon the man says, "I see a little.
When he points with only one finger and the man replies that he does not see, this is analogous to entering the True Dharma (Tattva).

Seeing the Buddha-nature with two fingers while not seeing it with one is an analogy for not seeing the Buddha-nature through either the two truths of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and conventionality (*saṃvṛti*).

When he points with three fingers and replies that he sees it "a little," this is an analogy for seeing the Buddha-nature within the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), which is the oneness of the three truths—emptiness, conventionality, and the middle.
According to the sutra, the skilled physician uses a golden scalpel to pierce the cataracts of the eye; pointing with one finger and so forth refers to this very process.
The analogy of the "Golden Scalpel" (*Suvarṇa-śalākā*) still pertains to the partial teachings (*pradeśa-dharma*).

Therefore, the Master of the Treatise further took the passage from the twenty-third fascicle concerning the Vajra-samādhi—which states that there is nothing it cannot shatter—and added the character "Vajra" (*vajra*) to the meaning within the context of the "Golden Scalpel.

Because the Vajra is a scalpel for piercing cataracts that is exceptionally sharp and differs from ordinary gold, it serves as a metaphor for the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-dharma*); only thus can the meaning be fully exhausted.
Now, following the text according to its meaning, we shall establish three points each for the subjective capacity (*neng*) and the objective referent (*suo*).

The subjective capacity is illustrated by the metaphor of the *vajra* probe, representing the principle and practice of the Perfect and Sudden teaching; the objective referent is illustrated by the metaphor of the cataracts of the eyes, representing the principle and practice of the partial and shallow teachings. Therefore, the text states:
"The golden probe of the perfect *i* [triad] is used to clear away the cataracts of ignorance of the four eyes, so that in all places one may see the *zha*."

Regarding that "finger" of Buddha-nature, some say it refers to the teaching (*śāsana*) because it elucidates the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), hence it is called the "perfect *ī*. It can shatter provisional doubts, and thus it is likened to a golden lancet (*suvarṇa-śalākā*) that pierces the cataract to allow one to see Buddha-nature; therefore, it is called the "three fingers. Is it not the case that the golden lancet merely serves as a metaphor for the teaching? Why, then, is it also used as a metaphor for practice (*caryā*) and principle (*tattva*)? Answer: If the teaching of the three virtues, which is capable of shattering biased attachments, is already compared [to a lancet], [how much more so are practice and principle]. Furthermore, the golden lancet is used as a metaphor for the teaching because it is able to remove the cataracts of sentient beings' ignorance. Practice is like the lancet because it is able to eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings. Principle is like the lancet because it is able to sever the delusions of sentient beings. Therefore, the three—teaching, practice, and principle—are all metaphorically designated as "fingers. This is why the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The finger is not the moon; the teaching is not the meaning. Thus, the three fingers are indeed a metaphor for the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle. This is why the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra* states: "The three fingers are the three aspects of the Dharma. How could it be detrimental to the meaning of the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel), which establishes the perfect contemplation for removing delusions and the pervasive penetration of the perfect principle to clear away the cataracts [of ignorance]?

Moreover, since the hearing of the teaching and the breaking of doubts must necessarily rely on the understanding of the principle, and the understanding of the principle must necessarily cultivate contemplative practice, I employ these three meanings to explain the *Vajra Scalpel*.
Furthermore, because within the perfectly integrated teachings the partial teachings are opened up to become the perfect teachings, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "All are for the sake of the One Buddha."
By means of the vehicle (*yāna*), there is the sense of resolving the teachings: opening up partial practice to establish perfect practice, as in "The path you all practice is the bodhisattva path";

this is the sense of resolving practice. By means of the principle (*tattva*), there is the sense of resolving the principles: opening up the gate of expedient means to reveal the true reality, as in "Opening the gate of expedient means to show the true aspect";
this is the sense of resolving principle. Question: Seeing the three fingers, one originally uses them as a metaphor for the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Regarding this principle, since it has already been illustrated by the analogy of the golden needle, how can one further explain the meaning of the "three fingers"?

To fully comprehend that ignorance is itself Buddha-nature is like using the golden needle to pierce away the cataract; this Buddha-nature is both one and three, which is precisely the meaning of the "three fingers.

One must certainly interpret the text according to its underlying meaning, rather than allowing the literal phrasing to obstruct the meaning. As for the initial metaphor of the teaching, it is similar to a hole bored in this world.

The second elder’s teaching speaks only of humans, animals, and so forth, who are born by receiving *qi* (vital energy), transmitting their physical forms in succession; these are the divergent doctrines of Western secular teachings (*yún yún*).

When the Buddha-dharma first arose, for those of the lowest capacity, it was taught as the Human-Heavenly Teaching (*rén tiān jiào*), clarifying that both the primary and secondary realms (*yī zhèng*) within the three worlds are all induced by the power of karma (*yè lì*).
Because good and evil karmas differ, one is induced into one of the six destinies (*liù dào*).
The distinctions between the primary and secondary [realms] are not yet discussed here, let alone the impermanence of all phenomena, much less the omnipresence of the Buddha-nature.
All of these are seen by the two eyes of flesh and heaven, which are like having cataracts completely covering the vision;

since one cannot even see a single finger when pointed out, how could one see three? If the two teachings of the *Zang* (Tripiṭaka) and *Tong* (Shared) merely discuss the mind giving rise to the six [consciousnesses],...

The Way relies on the Tripitaka to perceive the six realms as real and the common teaching to perceive them as empty; yet when one examines its great purport, it only explains the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Just as when the cataracts are first cleared, one points with a single finger to show the way, those who receive the teachings and practice attain only the Eye of Wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and do not see the Buddha-nature.

As the answer states, "I do not see," the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) then discusses the mind giving rise to the ten realms and the phenomena of the environment and inhabitants (*bhājanopapatti-dharma*), which must first be extinguished.

There are those who speak of entering nirvana without successive cessation and of emerging from nirvana into existence; though they discourse on the Buddha-nature inherent from the beginning, they do not know that it is primordially endowed with the three thousand realms.
Though they discourse on the wondrous principle of the Middle Way, they claim it is manifested only upon reaching the ultimate fruit.

If one examines their teaching, it merely explicates the two truths, like pointing with two fingers. Those who receive these teachings and practice them obtain only the two eyes of wisdom and dharma, yet fail to see the single thought-moment.

Regarding the three thousand [dharmas] as the true cause of Buddha-nature, it is as in the answer: "I do not see them. Generally speaking, although the various preceding teachings differ in depth, they have not yet discussed Buddha-nature;
since the Buddha-eye has not been attained, they are all like eyes obscured by cataracts.

That which is discussed in the Perfect Teaching—the three thousand in a single thought-moment, with no objects outside the mind, being simultaneously empty and middle, and the mutual identity of the three and the one—is like that "True Yi" (the character *yi* written with its components in their original form).
If the teaching flourishes, provisional explanations are simultaneously discarded; partial attachments are all dispelled, and the various obstructions naturally vanish.
Therefore, the present Perfect Teaching alone earns the name "The Golden Scalpel," for it is able to pierce the cataracts of ignorance regarding the four eyes across all teachings.

Although those who study the Mahāyāna possess only the physical eye, it is called the Buddha-eye; they perceive emptiness, the provisional, and the middle as clearly as seeing three fingers. Thus, the following passage demonstrates this.
For those who have not yet received the provisional teachings, the mind is inherently complete; thus, one pierces the film of ignorance over the two eyes of flesh and heaven.

For those who have already received the provisional teachings, the essence is complete according to their respective stages; thus, one pierces the film of ignorance over the two eyes of wisdom and dharma. Therefore, the text says:
"The golden pincers of the perfect *ī* are used to pierce the film of ignorance over the four eyes. Next is the analogy for the practitioner.

Receiving the worldly teachings, one cultivates the practices of the Five Constant Virtues and so forth; receiving the teachings of humans and devas, one cultivates the practices of the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Paths and so forth;

receiving the teachings of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* (Tripitaka and Shared) vehicles, one cultivates the contemplative practices of analyzing emptiness (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and realizing emptiness (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*); and receiving the Separate Teaching (*Pratyekabuddhayāna*), one cultivates the contemplative practices of the three successive insights.

All these aforementioned practices merely result in the attainment of the four eyes, which are entirely composed of ignorance—like a cataract over the eye. If one cultivates the Perfect Practice (*Ekayāna*), [the three insights]...
Contemplating the single mind constitutes the partial and shallow practice; the perfect and sudden practice consists of the four eyes, which are in fact the Buddha-eye.

Because one contemplates that ignorance itself is the Buddha-nature, it is now specifically compared to the "Vajra Scalpel," which is able to pierce the cataracts of ignorance over the four eyes and all other practices.
Regarding the three metaphors for principle: the worldly teachings, including those of the human and celestial realms, explain the mundane world.

The principle of the *Zang* (Treasury) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings elucidates the principle of supramundane true emptiness; the *Bie* (Distinct) teaching elucidates the principle of the three truths in sequential order;
and the comprehensive principle of all the aforementioned teachings is that which is seen by the four eyes—all of which are entirely obscured by ignorance regarding the Buddha-eye.

It is like not seeing the three virtues of Buddha-nature due to cataracts in the eye, as if one cannot see three fingers. If one perceives the perfect principle (*yuanli*), then one attains realization.
Ignorance (*avidyā*), in its very essence, is unchanging; the three thousand realms and the three truths are omnipresent in all places. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Because one sees the Buddha-nature, one cannot be bound by any fetters or afflictions. Therefore, the perfect principle is likened to a diamond probe (*vajra-kṣura*): it can resolve all partial and shallow principles.
It can pierce the film of ignorance so that one may see the finger of the Buddha-nature within the three truths. "Leaving behind" (*li*) means to depart from [the provisional].

The three characters correspond to the teaching, the practice, and the principle. Gold is a metaphor for the perfect principle; hardness is a metaphor for the perfect practice; and the chisel is a metaphor for the perfect teaching. Why is this?
The principle of Buddha-nature remains unchanging while following conditions, just as the essence of gold does not alter.

If one understands this principle and contemplates in accordance with it—where the three contemplations are unified within a single mind and subject and object are non-dual—then there is no delusion that cannot be shattered, just as gold possesses the quality of firmness and hardness.
Whatever one intends to strike with is shattered. By cultivating the single mind through the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), the contemplation merges with the object;

thus, one is able to explain what has been realized to others, causing them to destroy their delusions and understand the principle of the three truths (*tri-satya*). Just as a diamond serves as a surgical probe to remove cataracts from another’s eyes, allowing them to see the three fingers, the text says:
"Once, during a quiet night, I contemplated for a long time until I was unaware that I had even begun to snore."

Because phenomena possess their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), the character "Bi" (錍) is used as a metaphor for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). The preceding combined explanation was based on one's own practice (*zixing*): first the teaching, then the practice, and finally the principle;

that is, by receiving the teaching and cultivating contemplation, when contemplation is perfected, one accords with the principle. The subsequent separate explanation is based on transforming others (*huata*):

first the principle, then the practice, and finally the teaching; that is, relying on the principle to cultivate contemplation, when contemplation accords with the principle, one is able to [manifest] what is within one's own mind.

The exposition of the realization is presented for others; furthermore, because the sequential explanation follows the meaning of the title, the principle (*li*) is taught first and then separated for explanation.

Within this combined and separated explanation, the three meanings of essence (*ti*), function (*yong*), and practice (*xing*) are integrated: the *Ligongjingbei* (Diamond Scalpel of Principle) is the essence of Buddha-nature;
the *Xingjiaojingbei* (Diamond Scalpel of Practice) is the contemplative practice; and the *Jiaojingjingbei* (Diamond Scalpel of Teaching) is the refutation.

In the "Exegesis on Dispelling Delusion" (*Miyòng lǐshì*), the character for "gold" (*jīn*) symbolizes principle (*lǐ*, *tattva*); the character for "body" (*tǐ*) symbolizes practice (*xíng*, *pratipatti*); and the character for "awl" (*pí*) symbolizes teaching (*jiào*, *dharma*).

These three dharmas are fully encompassed within this general discussion. Question: The primary intent of this treatise is precisely to refute those who propagate Mahāyāna while clinging to the view that insentient things lack Buddha-nature (*wúxìng*).
Why, then, does it employ the Perfect and Sudden (*yuán-dùn*) to refute the partial and shallow (*piān-qiǎn*) interpretations?

Answer: Even if one were to expound the vast, perfect, and sudden teachings of the scriptures, if one does not understand that the three thousand [dharmas] are inherently complete and pervade all places, then it would entirely belong to partial understanding.

Yet even this [teaching] still grants [the truth] in its entirety; if one were to completely deny it, one would be no better than those of the Lesser Vehicle or the non-Buddhists, as stated in the text (etc.).
Question: For what reason is the title composed of only three characters, rather than being expanded?

Regarding the title, if one were to examine and investigate the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* through the analogy of the "Golden Scalpel" (*Jinbi*), then the "Golden Scalpel" would be the subject being evaluated, and thus the word "Treatise" (*Lun*) could be appended.
However, in this current text, the "Buddha-nature as the Three Causes" is precisely what is being evaluated;

therefore, it would be appropriate to title it simply the *Buddha-nature Treatise*. Nevertheless, in order to distinguish it from the ancient *Buddha-nature Treatise*, the present treatise is made manifest.

Because this critical treatise has the function of shattering delusion, it takes *Vajrasamādhi* as its title; thus, these three characters constitute the entire meaning of the word "treatise" (*śāstra*), and there is no need to further append the character for "treatise.
Question: If that is so, since other treatises also shatter delusion, could they not also be called *Vajrasamādhi*?
Answer: Since other treatises do not manifest that insentient things possess the Buddha-nature, how could they possibly merit such a title?
Furthermore, as for this title: since the preceding and succeeding works each establish their own names to distinguish them from one another, how could they be appropriately conflated into one?

Second, regarding "Buddha-nature as the essence": "essence" (tǐ) carries the meaning of the primary substance. In the treatise on the Buddha-nature of the Three Virtues, it is the primary substance that is discussed.
This Buddha-nature is precisely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The five aggregates do not transcend matter and mind; matter is constructed from the mind, and its entire substance is mind.
This capacity to construct is fully endowed with all dharmas. Therefore, it is pointed out that the momentary deluded mind itself is Buddha-nature.

This wondrous principle universally encompasses all things without excluding even insentient matter; this is precisely what is being discussed here as the primary essence, intended to make it manifest.

The three meanings are clarified as follows: first, the single nature; second, the measure of the essence; and third, the virtues of the essence. Regarding the "nature" (*gotra*): the three obstacles are themselves the three virtues.
Since the obstacle is the very seed of virtue—just as waves are the seed of water and water is the nature of the waves—it is called the "nature" (*gotra*).

Regarding the "measure of the essence": this mind-nature is neither internal nor external; it pervades empty space and is equal to the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas, like a finger [pointing to the moon].

Although one may wish to imitate the frown of the Sage, one likely does not know that the beauty of the frown lies in its cause. That which serves as the foundation for the Great Teaching below is precisely this:
the establishment of the perfectly interfused Great Teaching is intended solely to reveal this nature of the three thousand [realms] as the true cause.
It is not that the principle to be expressed arises only through the teaching that expresses it; for there is that which exists [prior to expression].
Therefore, the fact that one can possess merit depends ultimately on the ability to cause that which is cognizable; thus it is said that "merit lies herein.

The subsequent passage, which states, "If 'Mind-Only' were not established, all the Great Teachings would be entirely useless," conveys this very meaning. Regarding the section beginning with "The myriad streams," there are two parts:

first, the citation of a metaphor to provide an explanation. Second, the initial metaphorical exposition. The text says: "When water flows separately, it is called a 'stream' (pài); 'tú' refers to a path or way."
In Wang Biao’s *Fu on Water*, it is said: "It yields its bounty to form the four seas; it carves out channels to flow as the hundred rivers.

Now, although the ten thousand streams are distinct, they all originate from a single source; although the many currents differ, they all converge in the sea. Thus, the ten thousand streams are used as a metaphor for the teachings, and the many currents as a metaphor for practice.
The principle of Buddha-nature is like the source and the sea; the establishment of the teachings based upon that principle is like [the carving of channels].

The source arises from various branches; practicing to reach the principle is like streams returning to the sea. This "convergence" (*he*) is such that while the words of the text are concise, the meaning is vast.

Now, first I shall respond with metaphors, and subsequently provide a detailed explanation of the text. Regarding the convergence of all phenomena (*dharmas*), it is like the merging of ten thousand streams. Regarding the convergence of the great purport, it is like the meeting of common paths. Regarding the convergence of the cultivation of practice, it is like the joining of many currents.

Regarding the convergence of what is expected, it is like the returning to the ultimate destination. Next, I shall explain this in further detail. As for the phrase "the convergence of all phenomena":...
The general purport is this: it reveals that Buddha-nature is the foundation upon which all teachings rely; "all dharmas" refers precisely to these various teachings.

Since all partial and small (Hīnayāna) teachings rely upon this nature, when one reaches the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is nothing partial or incomplete, and all that was coarse becomes wondrous. Thus, we know that Buddha-nature is the great purport of all teachings.
This is discussed from the perspective of transcending the boundaries between vehicles (*kajie*); if, however, one speaks according to the specific divisions (*dangfen*), [it is as follows:]

The two teachings of the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) reveal only the partial truth; although the *Bie* (Separate) Teaching speaks of insentient beings, it remains separated from them. Thus, one knows that Buddha-nature exists only within the *Yuan* (Perfect) Teaching.

This is because throughout the beginning and end of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the three virtues are taught, and in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they are opened and revealed. Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, the three tracks (*triyāna*) are equally taught.
Because these three tracks are wondrous, it is called the *Wondrous Dharma*. The *Avataṃsaka* is the Dharma-realm, and the *Vimalakīrti* is liberation.
The *asādhāraṇa-prajñā* (unshared wisdom) and the "three thousand realms as the three truths in one essence" (*sanzen sandai ittai*) established by this school are not different;
if one understands this meaning, the present text can be understood. The Buddha-dharma of the ten directions is contained within a single kṣaṇa, and the great purport of all dharmas is seen herein.

Regarding the phrase "the goal of practicing cultivation," "cultivation" (*zō*) means to accomplish or achieve; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "to cultivate" (*zao*) means to bring to completion. Broadly speaking...

This refers to the profound realization that the Buddha-nature is the basis upon which all practices depend; thus, the cultivation and initiation of practices must necessarily rely upon the Buddha-nature.
However, while the term "cultivation of practices" generally applies to both the partial (Hīnayāna) and the universal (Mahāyāna), its true intent lies in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanrong). Why is this?

Because the practices of the partial and universal teachings accord with deluded sentiments; although each claims to be real, from the perspective of the Buddha’s original intention, they merely serve as a preparation for the Perfect.
It is merely a skillful means for the sudden teaching of Buddha-nature; therefore, when reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra, it is established in its true position and revealed.

Even a single snap of the fingers or the joining of palms becomes a cause for attaining Buddhahood. When you say, "That which you practice is the Bodhisattva path," you know that even those who cultivate practices within the partial or limited vehicles take Buddha-nature as their ultimate goal.
To speak precisely, however, this refers to a person of the Perfect Teaching cultivating the practices of the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
It is said that although the three types of practice differ, they all constitute the Buddha-nature; therefore, it is called "that which is aimed at.

Thus, the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) states that Tiantai transmitted from Nanyue three kinds of stopping and contemplation—namely, gradual, indeterminate, and sudden-perfect—which are all Mahayana and are collectively termed "stopping and contemplation.
They both take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their object, and the true mark is precisely the Buddha-nature. For this reason, there is gradual understanding and sudden practice.
The gradual and indeterminate [practices] involve sudden cultivation, while the sudden and the perfect-sudden involve both understanding and practice being sudden.

Although these three modes of practice differ, because their understanding is sudden, those at the initial stage simultaneously know the Buddha-nature; in the near term, they develop the stage of partial truth, and in the distant term, they reach the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment.
Therefore, it is said that this is what is expected through the practice of cultivation.
Question: For what reason are the two meanings provided as explanations for the practice of the teaching? Answer:

In the lower section on the dissemination of the Dharma (pariṇāmanā), for those who have already received the provisional teachings, the inherent nature is pointed out according to their respective stages of practice; therefore, the first meaning is required to explain the practice of the teaching.
For those who have not yet received the provisional teachings, the perfect interfusion is directly shown; therefore, the second meaning is provided to explain the practice of the teaching.

If it concerns the latter two sections of the introduction—teaching and practice—which are capable of revealing the Buddha-nature: first, it clarifies that teaching and practice possess the power to reveal [the nature].

Because one has faith in the teaching and looks up to the principle, hearing it enables one to contemplate; thus it says, "contemplate this" (*shi er si zhi*). Because one contemplates according to the principle, contemplation enables one to cultivate;
thus it says, "observe based on this" (*yi er guan zhi*). The *Yili* states: "Only after first realizing that the myriad dharmas are mind-only can one [proceed]."
"Contemplating the mind" is precisely this meaning. Furthermore, "reflecting upon it" refers to opening up understanding through the teachings as in the first six chapters of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*;
"practicing it" refers to correct cultivation based on that understanding, establishing practice according to insight. This is the Master’s own account.

If one follows what is elucidated by our own school—opening up understanding through the teachings and contemplating based on that understanding—then the principle of the non-differentiation of the three [aspects] is found herein.

One may resolve the doctrine that insentient things possess Buddha-nature so as to eliminate any grounds for doubt; therefore, the subsequent text states: "The *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) is the Dharma it inherits.

Thus, the two [sections] below concerning non-differentiation indicate the principle manifested through understanding and practice; the word "thus" (*ze*) is a term used to carry over from what precedes.
By relying on the teaching one attains understanding, and by relying on understanding one practices contemplation;

thus, one realizes that one’s own mind is endowed with the three thousand phenomena, and that each of those various Buddhas and sentient beings possesses the three thousand within their own ground of the mind. That "my three thousand" pervades "their three thousand," such that the three [spheres] are without distinction—this is what is meant.
The text contains six phrases: the first two phrases provide a general clarification, while the subsequent four phrases provide a specific demonstration. First, the general clarification:
This employs the terminology of both the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. The *Vimalakīrti* states: "The suchness of one is the suchness of all;

there is no duality. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* states: "Not a single form or a single fragrance is not the Middle Way. Regarding these, the first phrase clarifies the primary retribution (*vipāka*), while the second phrase clarifies the secondary environment (*bhājana-loka*).

The terms "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*) and "sages" (*ārya*) admit of multiple interpretations. "Ordinary beings" refers to the six classes of ordinary beings, while "sages" refers to the four classes of noble ones. Furthermore, "ordinary beings" may also refer to the nine [levels of existence].
Regarding the "sacred realm" (dhātu), those above the level of names—referring to the Perfect [Teaching]—are also subsumed within the Buddha-realm.

Furthermore, regarding "ordinary and sacred," within the Perfect [Teaching], the five stages of "immediacy" (pañca-avyavakīrṇa) are collectively termed "ordinary. Thus, while the five ordinary beings are discussed, the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha-samanvāgata-bodhisattva) is termed "sacred," and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is termed "virtuous" (bhadra);
the meaning is the same. Consequently, the nine realms and the five stages of immediacy are all termed the "Dharma of sentient beings" (sattva-dharma).
Only the ultimate fruit-Buddha is taken as "holy," which refers to the Buddha-Dharma itself. The first two [levels] are entirely not the intended meaning here;
although the latter [level] is precise, it also is not the intended meaning here. The intent of the present text is to facilitate easy understanding:

it provisionally uses the term "ordinary being" (*fan*) for the principle-as-such (*li-ji*) to refer to various sentient beings, and uses the term "holy" for the ultimate state to refer to those respective fruit-Buddhas. This statement regarding "sentient beings and Buddhas" refers specifically to their primary retribution (*zhengbao*).
Regarding "form and fragrance": these are the objects (*viṣaya*) that correspond to them; they are mentioned briefly as form and fragrance, but the intent includes the other four [sensory objects].

This refers to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) encountered by sentient beings and the six sense-objects encountered by the Buddha of fruition. These are called the "dependent retribution" (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the dusts for both sentient beings and Buddhas, created entirely by the mind.

Since the entire dust is the mind—that is, the phenomena are fully contained within the mind—it encompasses all things. Therefore, the immeasurable [qualities] of both sentient beings and Buddhas [are established therein].

Each of the three thousand worlds is complete within every single instance; though the phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and *pratishthā*) appear distinct according to their respective minds, when one now contemplates one's own mind, these three thousand worlds are subsumed therein without exception.

Understanding that those external environments and inhabitants are entirely constituted by the three thousand worlds of one’s own mind—which are simultaneously empty (*śūnyatā*) and the Middle Way—one speaks of "one suchness" (*eka-tathatā*) and "merging into purity. Thus, the minds of ordinary beings and the Buddha-mind mutually interpenetrate and encompass one another.

The same should be understood for the mind (*manas*). This passage correctly sets forth the principle that understanding according to reason and contemplation according to reason are non-differentiated;

it clarifies the tenet that the internal and external are not two. "Internal" refers to one's own mind, the three thousand realms; "external" refers to the three thousand realms within the minds of all sentient beings and Buddhas.
Thus, the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) states: "The 'other' refers to sentient beings; the 'self' is precisely the mind."
Furthermore, in the *Fenbie Gongde Pin* (Chapter on Distinguishing Merits), it is stated that "the external" refers to relying upon the form and mind of others (*yi-zen se-shin*).

Other passages may use the term "external" to refer to one's own form and so forth; however, this is merely a provisional explanation based on the phenomena themselves and does not definitively indicate the object of contemplation. Question:

Since the objects of the aggregates (*yin-jing*) in *Zhiguan* involve moving from the larger unit to the smaller—focusing specifically on the consciousness-mind (*shixin*) according to the underlying principle—and since the text further states that "one first contemplates the internal mind," [how do these accounts relate?]
Is it not the case that one's own physical body (*rūpakāya*) and its environmental support (*niśraya-vipāka*) both belong to the external? Answer:

This is merely because [the author] happened upon a passage in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* that distinguishes the objects of meditation, yet failed to fully grasp its underlying intent. Let us now attempt to discuss this.

The reason why *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* distinguish only the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is solely because all phenomena are transformations of the mind. Thus, the *Dà yì* (Great Meaning) states: "Form is created by the mind; its entire substance..."

Regarding the meaning of this "mind," the analogy states: one should know that all phenomena are differentiated by the mind; how could they ever claim to be identical or different of their own accord?
Therefore, the specific discernment of consciousness within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* still demonstrates this principle, stating: "First, contemplate the internal mind.
Once you have realized that this mind possesses the three thousand dharmas, you will see that your own body and environment (the *niśraya* and *pratishthā*) abide within the single mind."

Therefore, all texts consistently point to the three thousand realms within one mind as the "internal realm," while the various Buddhas and sentient beings, along with their environments and bodies, are termed the "external realm.
One should know that the three thousand realms within the internal mind are exclusively one's own environment and body;

thus, those who realize the three thousand realms as one mind must understand that the essence of principle (*li-ti*) is undifferentiated in its three aspects, which alone can be called the "oneness of ordinary and sage" and the non-duality of internal and external.

Secondly, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Furthermore, the student knows that their own inner mind possesses the three thousand dharmas, yet does not know that their own mind pervades those three thousand worlds;
it is likewise that each and every set of three thousand worlds mutually pervades one another. If one follows ordinary sentiments, one gives rise to views of internal and external;

one should instead illuminate that the essence of principle is fundamentally devoid of the four natures (*catuskoṭi*). Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. One who can know this..."
If one relies on a vague consciousness of the mind and, by inference, sees that there is a person who takes the three thousand realms as the internal mental essence—

regarding it as the internal self-substance and the self’s dependent retribution— and then designates both the Buddha’s and one’s own dependent and primary realms as "external," would this not be a failure to grasp the essential meaning and a deviation from the text?

Furthermore, if one were to rely solely on the passages in the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) concerning the selection of objects of contemplation without seeking their underlying intent, why [would such a view be necessary]?

Since the conditioned environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) and the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) are external, the minds of the other three aggregates should likewise be categorized as external. Any wise person should reflect upon this for a moment.

Furthermore, others rely on the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), which discusses the two types of creation—principle and phenomena—as well as the *Yili* (Exemplification of Meanings) and the passage on the "pervasive purification of the mind," to claim that although everything is "mind-only" in terms of doctrinal understanding (*jiao-kaijie*), when practicing contemplation (*guan*), one should contemplate only the internal.

The three thousand realms are created by the mind; they do not concern the creation of external objects. If one practices internal contemplation (adhyātma-vipaśyanā), there is fear that the mind will turn outward;

if one practices external contemplation (bahirdhā-vipaśyanā), there is fear that the mind will turn inward. For one who practices internal contemplation, it is necessary to wait until the principle (li) is manifested within;

once the principle is manifested, one uses this manifest pure mind to pervade all external phenomena. When these appear in a manner corresponding [to the principle], one then uses this correspondingly manifest pure mind to pervade them.

If it is the case that the manifestation of the principle (li) is likewise so when divided, then just as one must rely on external forms when practicing internal contemplation—waiting for the principle to manifest before a single particle of pure form can pervade the internal mind and other particles—it may be asked:
if the mind possesses the three thousand [realms] without regard for their phenomenal creation (shi-zao), then phenomenal creation would remain far removed from the mind;
the realm of principle would exist only within the body itself, which is identical to the externalist view of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka).
If this is indeed the plan for the fruit, then it is like the analogy of cutting down a tree to find its root or cauterizing a disease to find its source—it would be utterly useless. Why?

Because once the delusions within the mind have been extinguished and the principle made manifest, external forms are no longer relevant; one must employ a pure internal mind to traverse everywhere before the union [of subject and object] can be dissolved.
This is like cutting down a single root and yet finding that the branches and twigs remain entirely alive; one must then proceed to cut them all down.

If one must apply a thousand twigs before a single point can be cauterized to cure sixty percent of a disease, and if the disease remains entirely present, one must further cauterize until all six parts are reached for the hundred diseases to be cured;

since a thousand twigs are required to bring about full recovery, how can this be called "striking at the root"? Since the hundred diseases remain entirely intact, how can this be called "cauterizing the correct point"?
Is it not the case that the metaphorical intent of the *Zhi-guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) is not merely a hollow fabrication, but also clarifies the meaning of the present treatise?

All of this is merely a vain exertion; for now, according to the present treatise, based on the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*), the "three thousand [realms] in a single moment of thought" (*kṣaṇika-trisāhasra*) demonstrates that even grasses and trees possess the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, it says, "observing based upon [this realm]," and the subsequent text further states: "Now we establish that the essence of the *sattva*-cause is all-pervasive," and again:

"This is truly because from of old one has not skillfully and universally grasped the causal realm; rather, one observes oneself through the categories of self and other, and the dependent and the primary."

Regarding the mind and so forth, it further states: "To accept that the mind alone possesses [all phenomena], yet to doubt whether they exist or not, is to doubt the existence or non-existence of one's own mind. It also says:
"For one who realizes that the mind alone possesses the essence [of all things], how could there be difference or sameness?

Thus, even among the forty-six questions, all are shown to demonstrate that insentient beings possess the nature [of Buddhahood] by means of contemplating the mind as being fully endowed with the three thousand realms. Furthermore, the "Questions of the Wild Guest" asks: "How can the dependent [nature] be subsumed?"
Zhengyin answered: "The 'inconceivable realm' established by our school possesses the three thousand [realms] within a single thought-moment.
According to such passages, once one contemplates that the mind possesses the three thousand, one immediately realizes that insentient things have Buddha-nature.

How could it ever be the case that "principle-possessing" (li-jù) is unrelated to "phenomenal-creating" (shi-zào)? Furthermore, insentient grasses and trees are precisely what is created through phenomena. Moreover, the treatise begins...

In the end, it is simply said that by contemplating the "three thousand [realms] in a single thought-moment" (*ekacitta-trisahasra*), one already encompasses the "actualized creation" (*shizao*) as being inseparable from that single thought;

never at any point is it stated that one must first realize the manifestation of principle through contemplation before proceeding to the actualized creation. Question: If the actualized creation is integrated with the "principle-created" (*lizao*) through contemplation, why does the *Yili* (Exemplification of Principles) state:
"The sequence of cultivating contemplation must first involve the internal mind. If the internal mind is pure, then by means of this pure mind..."?
Question: "To universally traverse all phenomena is to spontaneously merge with them.

Since one must first use the internally pure mind to universally traverse all phenomena before speaking of 'merging,' does this not mean that when contemplating the principle (*li*), the phenomenal creation (*shi*) has not yet been integrated? Answer:

"The reason for first contemplating the internal mind is that the colors and forms of both the environment and its inhabitants are all created by the mind; their entire substance is mind. Therefore, one contemplates only the internal mind as it is inherently possessed."

The three thousand realms encompass all without exception; because they are simultaneously empty and middle, it is said that if the inner mind is pure, one has already realized that the mind possesses the three thousand realms.

Thereafter, in accordance with various objective conditions—whether regarding one’s own body and environment (*āśraya-dharmatā*) or the bodies and environments of other sentient beings and Buddhas—one realizes that none of these transcend the three thousand realms within my own mind.
Since the three truths and the three non-differentiations are without distinction, it is said that one "universally traverses" and "merges" [them].
Because they are unified, the *Zhancha jing* (Sūtra on Divination) states that one relies upon the single reality-realm (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*) to cultivate two kinds of contemplation:

first, the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*citta-mātra-vijñapti-bhāvanā*), which means knowing that all external objects are nothing but the mind; second, the contemplation of the true nature of suchness (*tathatā-bhūta-lakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*), which means contemplating that the nature of the mind is neither arising nor ceasing.

In the contemplation of suchness, one contemplates the principle; in the contemplation of consciousness-only, one traverses phenomena. Principle and phenomena are mutually identical, and these two contemplations are interdependent.

To gather the realm of the single reality is precisely the one mind, the three thousand realms, and the three truths. The contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the purification of the internal mind;

the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) is the thorough investigation of all phenomena. Thus, when the contemplation of True Suchness is perfected, one attains the Samādhi of the Tranquility of Mind;

when the contemplation of Consciousness-Only is perfected, one attains the Samādhi of the Tranquility of Form. One should know that although these two contemplations differ in their points of entry, that which they illuminate is the same.

The nature of mind and phenomena are of one essence and without distinction; since one must contemplate phenomena as being identical to principle, how could contemplating principle not include phenomena?

When others see the statement that "if the internal mind is pure," they immediately claim this refers to entering the stage of semblance-attainment (*sādharmya-samādhi*) or the stage of partial truth (*prativedha-bhūmi*), asserting that only thereafter can one universally traverse phenomena and perform creative acts;
such a view is profoundly erroneous. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) states: "What is called 'traversing' (*li*) means to inspect sequentially; how could it be divided [into stages]?"

When those at the stage of true reality examine and observe external objects, they only then dissolve [the distinction between subject and object) and merge with them; yet their errors are particularly numerous. Briefly stated, there are six:

namely, misrepresenting ordinary beings, slandering the sages, turning one's back on awakening, following delusion, deviating from the texts, and losing the essential meaning. This is because what the beginner contemplates—the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment—encompasses all things without exception; thus, in response to every objective circumstance, one realizes that everything is solely mind. Now, it is said: *Note:

The original text contains a complex critique of various erroneous views regarding the relationship between the practitioner and external phenomena within the Tiantai/Tendai tradition. The translation aims to preserve the technical terminology (e.g., *zhēnwèi*, *wàijìng*, *yīniàn sānqiān*, *wéixīn*) while rendering the philosophical argument into accessible English.*
If the beginner does not contemplate that phenomena are within the mind, then phenomena exist outside the mind, which is a mistaken view of ordinary people.

When the three thousand realms are manifested through partial revelation, their functioning is like images appearing in a mirror—spontaneously and universally pervasive. How could one wait until the mind that reveals them by parts has traversed everywhere before they merge and vanish?

This is to misrepresent the Sage. Those who are deluded perceive inner and outer as distinct; those who have awakened realize there is but the One Mind. If one were to claim that the inner and outer are suspended apart [as separate entities], it would be a grave error.

To follow [the principle of] "extraordinary" while being deluded is to reject the single mind’s universal encompassing; to turn one's back on awakening is to fail to realize that the principle is already manifest, only then beginning to traverse [the phenomena].
This treatise still discusses the internal endowment as fully encompassing the realm of phenomena;

if one were to claim that internal endowment has no relation to external phenomena and that they must first traverse them once the principle is manifest, this would contradict the texts. One merely sees that in the passages concerning the dual creation of principle and phenomena, the internal comes first.

Furthermore, if subsequent statements cannot be unified, one might claim that they are disjointed and lose their essential meaning. Since this error is significant, one may not realize how the text becomes prolix;
the two aspects of principle and phenomena will be explained in the following section.
Next, in the specific exposition, the first two phrases specifically demonstrate that the Buddha-mind of each respective fruit possesses the three thousand realms;
because this refers to the ultimate state, it is called "supreme sage" (*parama-ārya*). The text follows a principle of brevity, citing the weighty while omitting the light.

Within the ten realms, it specifically mentions the Avīci hell of burning and boiling—both the environment and its inhabitants—and yet these still fully reside within the Buddha-mind of the fruit; how much more so must this be true for the environments and inhabitants of the other nine realms?

How could it be otherwise? A single mind is fully endowed with the ten realms; since the ten realms are present, the hundred realms can be known, for each realm mutually contains the others and does not exceed these ten.
Furthermore, the phenomena of the hundred realms do not transcend the "basis" (āśraya) and the "supported" (adhiṣṭhāna), which are the three worlds:

the basis is the world of the land (*bhājana-loka*), and the supported consists of the two kinds of worlds—the provisional and the real. Within each instance of the basis and the supported, there are both causes and effects.

The principle of cause and effect within the fruits [of Buddhahood] does not transcend these ten "Thusnesses" (*tathatā*). Although the text briefly enumerates the fruit—the Buddha—it is fully present within the mind;

in reality, the three thousand realms (*sanqian*) are complete therein, and the meaning is perfectly manifest. The next two lines, beginning with "Vairocana," specifically demonstrate that each and every sentient being’s mind possesses the three thousand realms.
Now, by separately pointing to the phenomena of sentient beings, it indicates the stage of "principle-as-such" (*lizhi*).

The principle of "Identity with the Principle" (*li-ji*) subsumes a vast range of stages; although those at the initial stage of the Separate Teaching (*bie-jiao*) have not yet realized that the three thousand realms are one mind, they are nonetheless persons who are "identical with the principle.
Here, from among these persons identical with the principle, we specifically point to the mind within the realm of hell.

Vairocana refers to the body of the Buddha-realm, and the "Peaceful Light" (*ji-guang*) refers to the land of the Buddha-realm; since the dependent and the primary are non-dual, the body is itself the land.
Therefore, it is said that the body and land of Vairocana are identical; the land is the body, and thus one may also say that the Land of Tranquil Light (Jigō) is the body and land.
Although the four lands and the three bodies are non-dual in essence, here we refer to the Dharma-body and the Land of Tranquil Light by following what is supreme and focusing on the essence.

"To transcend" means that because the hells are situated below the six classes of ordinary beings, they are called "lower ordinary beings. The phrasing is also abbreviated, using the superior to illustrate the inferior, as is the case with the Buddha.
If even the most supreme realms and their inhabitants do not transcend the single thought-moment of a being in hell, how much less so for other realms and their inhabitants?
By analogy with what precedes, the "single mind" of the three thousand worlds can be understood accordingly.

Therefore, in this present text, when clarifying the Dharma of sentient beings, it specifically refers to the stage of "Li-ji" (the identity with reality), while its meaning extends through all stages; when clarifying the Buddha-Dharma, it specifically refers to the ultimate stage. Now, one realizes this within oneself.
The three thousand realms possessed by the mind are present within the minds of both sentient beings and Buddhas;

therefore, it is said that my "three thousand" encompass everything without exception. As the preceding text states: "If one observes them based on this [principle], then ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness.

Furthermore, because the Buddha’s mind possesses the hells' environment and its inhabitants due to the non-interruption of inherent evil (*śubha-dharmatā*), the mind of a hell-being likewise possesses the state of Buddhahood.
Because the body and the land arise from the uninterrupted nature of goodness, one should know that the three—sentient beings, Buddhas, and the Mind—are without distinction.

This is the structural framework for the contemplative path of "One Family" and the ultimate destination for the perfect understanding of all texts. Although there are three names, their meaning does not exceed two. Why?

Because when viewed from oneself toward others, "others" refers to sentient beings and Buddhas; since "self" is indicated as the primary point, it is called "Mind. Others [are so named] because they are distinct from it.

Regarding the statement "sentient beings [view] themselves as themselves, yet they are called sentient Buddhas," this refers to sentient beings in contrast to the other two [categories]. Furthermore, one must understand that each possesses the three thousand realms;
this means that the mind of oneself, the mind of sentient beings, and the mind of the Buddha each possess the three thousand realms. Why?

Because the self’s environment and body (the *ishō*), as well as the environment and bodies of sentient beings and Buddhas, are all created by the mind and are all possessed by the mind. Thus it is stated in the text.
Yunji says, "The mind of the ultimate sage is no different from a single thought of an ordinary person. It also says, "The minds of each and every sentient being are all-pervasive.

Furthermore, the *Fenbie Ermen* (Discriminating the Two Gates) states, "The three thousand realms are simultaneously present within the ground of the mind," and that "the three thousand realms in the Buddha’s ground of the mind are no different [from those in the sentient beings' minds].

All of these must point directly to the mind in order to assist the path of contemplation. Others do not understand this; although it is said that [all phenomena] are fundamentally based on the mind, they fail to grasp it. Even when it is said that [they are not...], [the meaning remains obscured].

It is merely that the mind creates the three thousand [worlds], and both sentient beings and Buddhas likewise create the three thousand; yet they do not realize that all these refer to the minds of sentient beings and Buddhas.
Furthermore, it is said that the lands inherently possess the three thousand, yet they do not realize that the lands are entirely the mind.

This is precisely the same as what follows below, where the deluded claim that grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles each have their own separate causes and effects. If one were to understand that the mind of sentient beings is the pervasive nature...

If it were universal, then the Buddha-nature of insentient things and the attainment of Buddhahood by insentient things would be clearly and easily seen; therefore, I request that you dispel your emotional attachments and read this text carefully.
Previously, in the second part of the separate preface concerning the causal origins, I established these points because I intended to reveal the Perfect Teaching and refute divergent arguments.
Speaking while dreaming and posing questions as a guest in the wilderness both rely on concrete events to clarify principles and use parables to express the Dharma.
This section is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the reason for posing the questions. "A tranquil night" refers to ignorance being like the night;

because one realizes through the three contemplations that ignorance is itself Buddha-nature, it is called a "tranquil night. Based on the understanding of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, one cultivates the practices of the three contemplations.
Having long practiced and studied this realization that the single mind is replete with the three thousand dharmas, it is said: "After a long time, he contemplated it.
The preceding passage stated that he had never failed to keep the meaning of Buddha-nature in his heart; because his moment-to-moment perfect contemplation was uninterrupted, it is said:

"His contemplation did not cease. One might ask: "The previous explanation was correct, but since 'contemplating' was already discussed in relation to opening the understanding (*kaigai*), why is it mentioned again here as 'after a long time'?"
Question: Why did you compose the *Xiuguan shi* (Explanation of Cultivating Contemplation)? Answer: Since I have long understood this principle, how could I not cultivate contemplation?

Therefore, by using "long-term reflection" (*jiu si*), I indicate the practice of contemplation (*guanxing*). The subsequent passage rebukes the "wild guest," stating: "This is truly because from of old one has not been skilled at universally grasping the contemplations of cause and effect and so forth within one's own mind.
Since he rebukes others for not contemplating while clarifying his own contemplation, it is evident [that I do so]. Furthermore, as stated previously...

The text says: "Relying upon it, one contemplates it. Furthermore, if one is at the initial stage of practicing the sublime contemplation (*miao-guan*), one is still a person at the level of names and designations;

if the path of contemplation has already been perfected, one is then a practitioner who contemplates the Way. Between these two paths—progressing or regressing—I do not yet dare to take a definitive position;

it is as if one were dazed in sleep, or perhaps like the state of *yanran* (a state of profound, ineffable stillness). This refers to the fact that the ultimate principle is quiescent and extinguished, fundamentally beyond verbal expression, and is not... [the text here appears to be incomplete].
For the sake of those deluded disciples, one forcibly engages in question and answer, establishing the roles of guest and host as mere conventions.
This is like the fact that the mind is fundamentally without the phenomena of dreaming; yet when the mind encounters these phenomena, it constitutes a dream.

Just as the mind awakens to itself, sleep is used as a metaphor for delusion, and waking represents enlightenment. Because of delusion, there is the distinction between the sentient and the insentient; in enlightenment, there is only the single nature.
Now, as for the term "insentient" (*wuqing*), the phrasing may appear to be delusory; yet, since it is said that they possess a nature (*xing*), it is not actual delusion.

It is like being in a state of *huanghu* (vague confusion), which resembles sleep but is not actual sleep; hence it is said, "vaguely as if asleep. Although both interpretations are applicable, the former meaning is correct.
Regarding the phrase "unawareness and somnolence" (*bujue yiyun*): *yiyun* (somnolence) is pronounced *niushi* (反); according to the *Tongsu Wen*, speaking in one's sleep is called *yiyun*.
"Moon-sleep" (*wénmián*) refers to speech; it is deluded talk that does not perceive the categories of sound. Some write the character "art" (*yì*) instead, but this is not what is used here.

Because one speaks without having said anything, it is called "unawakened" (*bùjué*); because one says something while there is nothing to say, it is called "sleep-talking" (*nièyún*). Regarding the claim that "insentient things possess nature":

if one were to proceed solely from the perspective of awakening, one would simply say they "possess Buddha-nature" (*fóxìng*) as a principle, without discussing whether they are sentient or insentient. This is like...

Regarding what is taught in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong): if one were to address delusion exclusively from a single perspective, one would merely distinguish between the "basis" (the environment) and the "supported" (sentient beings), without discussing the principle of Buddha-nature;
this is as discussed in the partial teachings (pianjiao). Now, when it is said that insentient things lack [sentience] yet possess nature, there are two intended meanings:
first, to show that delusion originally arises from the transformation of nature, and thus they are called "insentient"; second, to show that nature [itself] enables them to undergo transformation.
Because they are deluded, it is said that "there is a nature"; this is intended to make one realize that the insentient objects they grasp are entirely the nature of their own mind.
Therefore, this single phrase serves as the fundamental basis for raising the inquiry that constitutes the main body of the treatise.

Next, regarding the second section which clarifies those who pose the questions, there are two parts. First, it describes that although the single nature is all-pervasive, those who are deluded do not know it in their daily lives;
thus it says, "Suddenly seeing a person. Being lost in reality and clinging to the provisional, their minds wander outside of principle;

therefore, they are called "wild guests" (*yake*). Regarding their "appearance and demeanor" (*rong-i*), this refers to their conduct and deportment, meaning their dignified bearing. Second, it describes their external appearance; "appearance and demeanor" refers specifically to their physical presence and behavior, which is to say, their *vīrya* (dignified bearing).

The *Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiaojing*) says: "Their deportment is worthy of observation; their advances and retreats are measured. The *Odes* (*Shijing*) say: "The virtuous person, the noble gentleman—his demeanor is without error.
Now, because his advances and retreats have lost their order and his dignified bearing has become erroneous, it is said he is "coarse and *kuàng*. *Kuàng* (古猛) means fierce or strong.

The *Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters* (*Shuowen Jiezi*) states that *kuàng* refers to a dog that cannot be approached. It is also written as *kǔ* (穬), meaning the awns of grain. *Kǔ* is not the correct character form for this context. Advance.
To "retreat" (tui-xia) here indicates a display of coarse and unruly behavior; it is easy to say that "advancing and retreating are not constant," yet this does not mean leaving the group.
Now, I merely borrow these words without adopting their original meaning. This phrase serves as a general prelude for the external deportment discussed in the subsequent text.

In the present text, "pressing forward to stand level" refers to advancing, while in the subsequent text, "respectfully retreating and kneeling at sunset" refers to retreating. Because exercising power is difficult to realize in its true essence, [this is stated].
It is said that because one presses forward while relying on intellectual understanding to disparage others, it is called "standing level.

This refers to the remaining two sections of the main body of the text, which are divided into two parts. First, the section on the reciprocal questioning and challenging that correctly demonstrates the meaning of the Buddha-nature’s pervasiveness.

Fourth, the section that correctly describes the Buddha-nature of insentient beings. Sixth, the section that poses a general question to determine what was previously stated; [the character] "shu" (述) below should be [treated as such].
Regarding the character "xié" (邪), there are instances where it is written as "zé" (作);

this is an error. I said: "The following two [points] are answered briefly to show that what is appropriate is not empty. This means that what was previously stated—that insentient things possess the nature [of Buddhahood]—is indeed true.
The *Fānyǔ* (方言) states: "Kuā yū rán. Guo Pu’s commentary says: "These are all responsive sounds. "Kuā" is pronounced as "huā guā" (呼瓜反).
"U" (pronounced as in "gan"). The guest said:
"The last three sections concern the provisional texts of the Great Sūtras; it is truly an honor to be so humbled.

'Root source' refers to the principle being expounded, which is precisely Buddha-nature. 'Humbly seeking' and 'thinly investigating' are both terms of humility. This school speaks extensively of Buddha-nature."
"None shall transcend Nirvana at the Twin Forests" refers to the Śāla grove—translated as "Firm and Solid"—located in the city of Kuśinagara.

Because there are two trees on each of its four sides, it is called the "Twin Forests. When the Buddha was about to enter Nirvana, on the morning of the fifteenth day of the second month, he summoned the assembly from within this grove with a sound and light, expounding the doctrine of the eternal and extensively discoursing upon the ultimate perfection; therefore, it is called his "final" [teaching].

Because this is the proclamation of the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), it is called the ultimate discourse. Yet you claim that even insentient things possess [Buddha-nature]; however, that sutra states:
"That which is not Buddha-nature is designated as Buddha-nature for the sake of [certain beings]. By "that which is not Buddha-nature," it refers to walls, tiles, and rubble.
Such sacred words have a basis upon which they rely. You alone now claim that insentient things possess nature, which abruptly contradicts the sutra. Indeed!
Because it is difficult to believe and follow, it is called "benevolence" (*ren*); why speak only of "equality"? I replied:
"The latter four [categories] distinguish between the Great and the Small. This answers the two [points]. First, I cite the ancient to raise a hypothetical objection.

Regarding the "ancient," the Dharma masters of old did not wish to specify their names, but merely referred to them as "the ancients. As the subsequent text says, "the people of the world," and so forth.
All are thus. Regarding the term *icchantika*, the Great Sūtra explains it through seven meanings. First, it states that *icchan* means "faith" (*śraddhā*) and *tīka* means "not possessing";

because they do not possess faith, they are called *icchantikas*. Next, it explains the term *icchan* by way of wholesome skillful means, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, impermanence, goodness, and so forth;
the explanation of *tīka* is as extensive as in the first phrase. Thus, the single name *icchantika* encompasses a multitude of meanings.
I lament that the virtuous masters of old did not see this translation; only Dao Lang of Hexi translated it as "extreme desire" (*jìyù*), meaning the limit of extreme evil desire.
Some say that if one lacks faith, the remaining meanings are lost. Since it encompasses all manner of evils, it cannot be translated partially.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "That which is most extremely evil is called an icchantika. An icchantika is a sentient being.

The ancients even spoke of "those without nature" (*amūla-gotra*), yet when they cited the scriptural passage stating that walls and tiles have no nature, they considered it insufficient grounds for reproach.
However, the ancients all observed that many scriptures clarify that *icchantikas* cannot attain Buddhahood and speak of their lack of roots of goodness;

thus, they referred to them as being "without nature. Yet, if one possesses even a momentary thought, the three thousand realms are fully present, and the nature of the true cause (*tathāgatagarbha*) is complete—how could this be so?
How much less could it be otherwise when the sutra text itself states that all sentient beings and even icchantikas possess Buddha-nature, or says that Buddha-nature exists in icchanticas?
This is merely because they have not cultivated wholesome roots; thus the sutra says that by reforming evil and cultivating goodness, one may attain the Way.
However, the following two [sections] demonstrate the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, explaining the teachings of the Great and Small Vehicles in contrast.

The provisional and the ultimate differ according to their respective capacities and circumstances, and thus what they teach varies greatly. The Lesser Vehicle teachings state that outside of mind there exist insentient realms such as grasses and trees, and thus do not discuss the Buddha-nature.
Scriptures such as the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* and the *Āgamas* belong to this category. The Great Vehicle teachings, however, state that the nature of sentient beings is all-pervasive;
outside of mind there is no objective realm, and not even a speck of dust is excluded. This is as taught in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna*.

Because the *Saṃyuktāgama* and other sūtras [teach] the Lesser Vehicle, the name "Buddha-nature" is excluded; because the Great Vehicle [teaches] that the insentient is extinguished, the designation "insentient" is eliminated.

However, this was merely a provisional classification of the categories of the Great and Small Vehicles to determine existence or non-existence in response to the secondary objection of the "wild guest.

When we reach the section on "Receiving and Understanding," where he requests a discourse on the Four Teachings, only then will the Four Teachings be applied in detail to distinguish between the sentient and the insentient.
Therefore, we know that the statement "the Great Teaching lies in the perfection [of the Small]" implies that the term "Small" encompasses both the Shared and Distinct [teachings].

A guest asked: "Regarding the citation of the Great Teaching to refute the confusion with the Small—[it is argued that] the Small Teaching does not discuss Buddha-nature, while the Great Teaching does not speak of insentient things.
Since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is precisely the Great Teaching, it ought to speak exclusively of Buddha-nature; why then [is this said]?"

Therefore, it is also said that insentient things [are not included]; since these two meanings are presented together, where would the distinction lie? Thus it is asked: "How can they be listed side by side? I replied:

Regarding the six sections below, which cite scriptural passages to demonstrate the meaning, there is a broad answer in three parts. First, a general refutation and statement of intent: "O you who are at leisure... [and so forth].

Yaya says that "practice" refers to the Buddha-nature, which consists of the three causes. Since the scriptural text within the *shijiao* (the teaching of ultimate reality) speaks only of the "direct cause," it is said "yes";
because it does not clarify the "conditional" and "developing" causes, it is said "no. Regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects of the doctrinal sections:

the ultimate direct cause is explained as being pervasive throughout all things, whereas the provisional conditional and developing causes are said to be excluded from tiles and stones. Therefore, although the *Nirvāṇa* section is great, [it is limited in this regard].
Since the teachings within the various schools possess both provisional and ultimate aspects, the three causes discussed in the ultimate teaching may be present or absent;

if one familiarizes oneself with this principle, one will ultimately not harbor doubts regarding the differences between the schools. For now, I shall briefly set forth the intent of establishing these doctrines;
