as for the detailed citation of scriptural passages to distinguish their similarities and differences, my purpose is to enable future generations who delight in discerning distinctions to [penetrate] the walls and tiles.

The explanation regarding stones proves that those who are insentient and devoid of nature have well grasped the purport of the Great Sūtra concerning the provisional and the real, and the progression and regression of these truths.
Having attained this purport, one understands that the discourse on tiles and stones is provisional while the metaphor of empty space is real;

thus, one does not obscure the true cause of the Real Teaching—that the principle of nature pervades all things. Consequently, one realizes that the doctrine I have established accords with the fundamental tenets of the Sūtra.
The "root cause" (zhengyin) is the primary and the principal; although the category involves provisional means, it takes the true teaching as its core and the root cause as its foundation.
Therefore, clarifying the pervasive nature of the root cause here accords with the central tenet of the sutra.
Now, regarding the establishment of the two markers and the formulation of the thesis that accords with the intent of the sutras:

"Now, establish," etc., refers to the "inconceivable realm of the three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment" established at the beginning of the section on the five aggregates in the fifth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

One should know that this text represents the definitive intent transmitted within this school; since the Master [Zhiyi] formulated his understanding and cultivated his contemplation based upon that text, he establishes it here.

This passage establishes the doctrinal tenets of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun) school and demonstrates that insentient things possess the Buddha-nature (*gotra*), based upon those texts. Regarding "sentient beings" (*sattva*):

this term distinguishes them from wood and stone, meaning that even a mere flicker of mind is fully endowed with the three thousand realms (*sanqian*). Since there is nothing outside these three thousand realms, both the subjective (the sentient) and the objective (the insentient)—the dependent and the primary—are equally included;

therefore, it is said that the essence of the True Cause (*zhengyin*) is omnipresent. Although the nature inherently possesses the conditions and the understanding (*yuan-liao*), they have never yet been activated since beginningless time.

Because it is the mental application (*citta-prayoga*), it is given the same name as the direct cause (*hetu*). Since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* text correctly discusses this nature whose substance and magnitude are all-pervasive, it uses empty space as a metaphor for it.

One should know that the establishment by our school that the minds of sentient beings possess the three thousand [realms], thereby encompassing both the environment and its inhabitants, is a profound penetration of the Buddha’s intent. Those who study this teaching, however, being ignorant of its intent, see only...
Regarding the statement that "form consists only of fragrance and color, and there is no dharma apart from them," this indicates a failure to understand that the substance of form and mind are one.

Consequently, they claim that grasses, trees, and the lands inherently possess the three thousand realms, without seeking the meaning of the text from beginning to end. Furthermore, as seen in the opening of the current passage where the fundamental tenet is established, it says:
"The essence of the correct cause of sentient beings is all-pervasive," and later, when the "wild guest" attains understanding, he still says: "It is simply... [the same].
Because the mind of sentient beings is pervasive and their nature is pervasive, all general discussions found in the intermediate sections of the text can be understood accordingly;
how much more so when it is explicitly stated that "form is mind," and that "a single speck of dust and a single mind are the very nature of the minds of all sentient beings and Buddhas.
Is this not precisely a discourse on the fact that the minds of sentient beings universally possess the three thousand realms? Therefore, the *Zhi Guan Fa* [Xiao Zhiguan] says:

The *Suximing* (Heart-Clarifying Commentary) carefully distinguishes between the essence of plants and trees and the lump of flesh, selecting only the mind that perceives and knows, extending even to the wondrous realm of right contemplation;
yet it still points to the *vijñāna*-mind as the basis for recording the text. Furthermore, it states: "By means of arising, one manifests what is possessed.

If the three thousand realms were inherently possessed by the land itself, then plants, trees, tiles, and stones should also possess the arising of mind. This would be precisely the same as the "ordinary beings" refuted in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Now, sentient beings claim that the Buddha-nature exists apart from the aggregates (skandhas). However, throughout the Mahāyāna teachings of a single lifetime, it is solely the nature of mind that is discussed;
thus it is said, "All who possess a mind shall become Buddhas," and again, "In the triple world there are no separate dharmas; it is created by the one mind alone.
Furthermore, it is said that although immeasurable dharmas are taught as being the Buddha-nature, they do not exist apart from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
For this reason, the holy records do not bestow [the name of "mind"] upon tiles or stones, yet they do not slight them; they honor all sentient beings through ritual alone.

Within the single family of the Perfect Teaching, one cultivates the contemplation of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) and even extends it to the nine objects, all of which are termed "mind. As it is said: "affliction-mind, illness-mind, karma-mind," and so forth.
The analogy of felling a tree by reaching its root is truly worthy of belief. Yet, even while gazing upon these holy words, people remain deluded.

This is truly deeply lamentable. Question: If you do not allow that grasses, trees, and so forth inherently possess the Three Thousand Worlds (*trichiliocosm*), for what reason does the seventh fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) apply the Ten Vehicles (*daśayāna*) to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), and then extend this by analogy to the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and objects encountered through conditions, stating that whether it be form (*rūpa*) or fragrance (*gandha*), all equally "possess the Dharma"?
Answer: At the beginning of that text, regarding the objective realm of the aggregates, it first...

It is shown that the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is able to create all phenomena; yet this creator is precisely this deluded mind, which, by virtue of the principle of the Three Truths (*tri-satya*)—in which all phenomena are inherently present—is able to universally create them.
Therefore, in the subsequent text, it is shown that the nature of the mind (*citta-prakṛti*) inherently possesses the three thousand realms (*tri-sahasra*).

Since form is entirely mind, one knows that the three thousand realms of the consciousness-mind encompass all phenomena exhaustively. At the end of the ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*), the same applies to the remaining [categories].

The discussion of the realms (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) is intended merely to harmonize all phenomena and demonstrate that the objects of contemplation are universal. This is all the more so for the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) and bases;

whether it be form (*rūpa*) or fragrance (*gandha*), these are simply the objects of the aggregates. Since the text’s initial explanation clarifies that the phenomena created by the consciousness-mind are entirely form, which is itself mind, what hindrance is there to the fact that each instance of form and fragrance is fully endowed with all phenomena?
One should know, therefore, that the endowment of form is the endowment of mind. Thus.

The principles and examples clarify that what is discussed as "perfect interpenetration" (yuanrong) means that the three locations—namely, the internal mind, internal form, and external form—are fully endowed with all phenomena (*dharmas*). Therefore, it is said:
"Once one knows they are fully endowed with phenomena, all phenomena are universally subsumed; how could they be separated from form?

Since form is subsumed within the mind, and the mind itself is form, one should know that for a person of perfect realization who knows the mind is endowed with the three thousand realms, how could external form be excluded? That the ultimate aim lies in "Mind-only" and "Form-only" is precisely the point here.

Question: If you do not admit that solitary grasses and trees inherently possess the three thousand [dharmas], but rather maintain that one must realize that form (*rūpa*) is precisely mind (*citta*) before they can possess these dharmas, then the dharma of form would merely be the "approacher" (*gantṛ*) and not the "approached" (*gamya*).

How then should one interpret the Sūtra which states, "All dharmas approach form"? Answer: Since form is identical to mind, form is itself the "approached. Thus, both the "approacher" and the "approached" are mind.

Question: How do their natures differ? If waves and water mutually contain one another, there is nothing that is not the moisture of water. Question: The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) cites the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*), saying:
"It is not only consciousness-only, but it is also precisely form-only. Furthermore, for those in the lower realms who are attached to form, they are enjoined to contemplate the mind;

for those in the upper realms who are attached to the mind, they are enjoined to contemplate form. Is this not because the form of the dependent retribution and so forth inherently possesses the three thousandfold world? Answer: Since it is said they are "attached to form," [it implies the following].

Those who harbor attachments do so merely because they falsely conceptualize and cling to the distinction between form and mind; thus, they engage in acceptance and rejection without realizing that internal and external forms are entirely one's own mind.

Therefore, when contemplating form, one should simply realize that form is itself mind—that the three thousand realms are inherent in form, which is the very same as the three thousand realms being inherent in mind.

Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) cites the *Śmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* to correctly demonstrate that in both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whether following conditions or confronting objects, [the practice] is always present.

Since the general meaning of this sublime principle states that form is created by the mind and that its entire substance is mind, one should understand that both conditions and objects are what is created, and are all identical to the mind.
Moreover, the supplementary text itself concludes: "The mind is *bodhi*, the liberation of all Buddhas;
seek it within the activities of the mind. Since form is identical to the mind, why do you stubbornly remain deluded? I ask you, O Assistant: [Explain this!]

Since it has already been stated that practice is neither merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) nor merely matter (*rūpa-mātra*), if one now claims that all matter is mind and only then speaks of the "endowment with dharmas" (*dharmopeta*), how does this differ from other schools that speak only of "consciousness-only"? Answer:

Since our school clarifies that the nature of mind is fully endowed with all dharmas, and since these dharmas are universally encompassed without being separated from matter, we are able to discourse through circular transformation; thus, we speak of "matter-only."
It is only because fragrance and so forth are entirely the mind's nature, inherently possessed from the beginning, that [the text speaks of them].

Others speak only of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) because they grasp only the meaning of the mind arising; thus, their teaching lacks the expression "only form and so forth. An analogy states:

although others claim "all is consciousness-only," they do not realize that the body and the land reside within a single thought-moment. When the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* discusses Buddha-nature, it says it is "not internal."

Question: When [the *Mohe zhiguan*] states that "neither external cessation-and-contemplation reveals the three thousand [realms]" and then says "neither cause nor condition," you now specifically establish the internal cause—the dharmas inherent in the mind.

Is this not contrary to the scriptures and in violation of the teachings? Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Neither internal nor external," precisely because it indicates that all things without exception are the nature of the sentient being's mind.
Therefore, one must not interpret cessation-and-contemplation as being exclusively internal or exclusively dependent on external conditions; rather, the text correctly demonstrates both.
The mind possesses the three thousand realms, pervading all things without exception; it cannot be said that this applies only to internal causes or external conditions.
Rather, this is done to demonstrate that the substance of the mind-nature is all-pervasive, thereby dispelling attachments and eradicating deluded thoughts. Why is this so?

For those deluded followers, it is shown that "all phenomena are created by the mind" and "all phenomena are entirely the mind. Once one realizes that everything is truly Mind-Only, there is nothing else to rely upon or oppose; it is simply Mind-Only.

Furthermore, since internal and external are both obliterated, how could there be anything that exists? Thus, the text says: "If one speaks of the existence of nature, it would be inconsistent to speak of insentient things. It also says:
"To realize that all is mind alone and to understand that the essence is inherently complete—how could there be difference or sameness?

One must not misinterpret passages such as those in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and claim that tiles and stones each possess their own inherent capacity for the Dharma based on the principle of the mind. The meaning of these words is clearly manifest in the *Nirvāṇa*.
It is said that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space; is this not because the nature of sentient beings is all-pervasive?

The *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) states that "with even a minute thought, the three thousand realms are fully present. Since it distinguishes plants and trees as being without mind, is this not because the nature of sentient beings is all-pervasive?

Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of form in the higher realms as clarified in the *Smṛtyupasthāna*, this is merely intended to cause sentient beings to cultivate contemplation and realize for themselves that external objects are [empty].
If it were not the case that form is one's own mind, then grasses and trees would each possess their own Buddha-nature and each have their own cause and effect. Alas!

It is easy for glue to stick to the hand, but difficult for sleep and dreams to awaken one; having already been obscured by the single mind, one ultimately ends up with two divergent schools. Question:

If you do not allow that grasses and trees inherently possess the three thousand [realms], then as for the *Zhiguan*, since it already allows for the contemplation of the mind, yet one still does not awaken—how is this?

If one contemplates form, and if form is itself the mind, what further is there to contemplate? The answer is: should there be such a karmic opportunity where it is appropriate to contemplate form, this is precisely to realize that form is the mind.
How could one see that because their suitability or preferences differ, one must then claim that mind and form are eternally distinct?

For example, if one practices contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and does not achieve awakening, one is instructed to practice tranquility (*śamatha*); if one practices tranquility and does not achieve awakening, one is instructed to practice contemplation. How could this be so?
The essence of cessation is free from contemplation, and the essence of contemplation is itself cessation; is this not so?

Furthermore, for those who do not enter through the gate of non-arising, one causes them to rely on the gate of arising—how could the essences of these two gates not be mutually identical? One should know that although mind and form are simultaneous, form is constructed by the mind and its entire substance is mind;
therefore, when contemplation reaches the creator, one sees all dharmas, for all dharmas are entirely [mind].
Because it concerns the mind, the first four of the ten methods for contemplating the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*) are restricted solely to consciousness and the mind;

they are not "too few. From the sections on "Obstacles and Penetrations" (*tsung-sai*) onward, they fully encompass all five aggregates; yet they are not "too many," because by focusing solely on the consciousness that acts as the creator, all phenomena produced by it are thereby subsumed.
As the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practices) states: "In order to harmonize all phenomena and demonstrate the pervasiveness of the object of contemplation, [the text] does so."
The following text illustrates the remaining *dhātus* and *āyatanas*. If one discusses the essence of their objects, contemplating the mind alone is sufficient.

Regarding "passage" (*tong*) and "obstruction" (*se*) and what follows, although it fully employs the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), all phenomena that are produced are [ultimately] the producers themselves. As the *Fuxing yu* (Explanations of the Supplementary Practices) states:

"The aggregates do not depart from the mind; the mind does not go beyond the aggregates. The aggregates follow that which can cover; the mind follows that which can produce. The producer is proximate while the covering is remote; both take the mind as their basis."
Objects of perception consist of both the contemplation of mind and the contemplation of form; although their modes of engagement differ, one realizes that all phenomena are nothing but mind.

Therefore, if one contemplates the single mind, it encompasses all things. One should know that if sentient beings do not understand the pervasive nature of the mind, yet claim that grasses and trees inherently possess the three thousand realms based on such an interpretation, their desire to realize the Way is like searching for a vulture’s nest.
To seek a phoenix while perched in a nest, or to catch a whale within a pit, though undertaken with the utmost diligence, is not its proper domain.

Thus, the three sections below and the three inductions clarify the meaning through the scriptures; this consists of two parts: first, clarifying the presence or absence of Buddha-nature and the provisional or ultimate nature of the scriptural divisions;

second, first clarifying the presence or absence of Buddha-nature, and then clarifying the provisional or ultimate nature of the scriptural divisions. Presence or absence refers to the Dharma, while provisional or ultimate refers to the teachings.

However, within the discussion of "advancement and non-advancement," the teachings of the provisional and the real are not unclear; and within the discussion of the provisional and the real, the dharma of the three causes is not unclear. Why is this?

It is because without the provisional and the real, there would be no means to determine advancement and non-advancement; and without advancement and non-advancement, there would be no means to manifest the provisional and the real.
First, the clarification of the advancement and non-advancement of Buddha-nature has three parts: first, the direct citation of the scriptural text to provide a detailed exposition of its meaning.
Section Two: Quoting Scriptures to Demonstrate the Meaning of the True Cause. Subsection One: Clarifying the True Cause of Sentient Beings. Part One: Quoting the Scriptural Text. [Note:
The character "十三" (thirteen) is an error for "三十一" (thirty-one), as it appears in the thirty-first fascicle. Now, this scripture exists in two versions, Northern and Southern.
Initially, Dharmakṣema translated it in the third year of the Xuanshi era of the Northern Liang dynasty, completing it in forty fascicles, totaling ten [sections].

The three-fascicle version was transmitted to the north and is thus known as the "Northern Text" (*Beiben*). During the Song dynasty, Emperor Wen issued an edict for Huiyan, Huiguan, and Xie Lingyun to jointly revise and finalize it;
this resulted in twenty-five chapters organized into thirty-six fascicles, which circulated in the south and is thus known as the "Southern Text" (*Naben*).
The current Southern Text is circulated separately outside the canon, and the commentaries and records of one school frequently cite its scriptural passages.
Regarding the citation of volume numbers, the Southern edition is taken as definitive.
There are those who, being unaware of this, merely consult the Northern edition and, seeing that the volume order differs, often claim that the references in the commentaries are erroneous.

The passage on the analogy of space cited here is, in fact, from the third volume of the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* in the Southern edition; it records the Buddha’s response to Kāśyapa’s objection, beginning with the word "one."
Although all sentient beings are impermanent, their Buddha-nature is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Therefore, in this sutra I say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither internal nor external, just as space is neither internal nor external.
If space possessed an interior or exterior, space could not be called "one" or "eternal," nor could it be said to be one.
"Wherever there is a location, there is empty space. Although it is neither internal nor external, all sentient beings possess it. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
When the sutra says that empty space is neither internal nor external, it means that empty space pervades all places;
it is not only within the bodies of sentient beings, nor is it only outside the bodies of sentient beings."—one word [sums it up].

That space, as both the environment and its inhabitants, encompasses all sentient beings such that they all possess it, means that within the bodies of all sentient beings there exists the great element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*).
Since sentient beings exist in other locations, how could space not exist in those other locations? If it were absent, it would not be called "space.
As for the correspondence with the Dharma: because Buddha-nature is not among the six sense organs, it is not internal; because it is not among the six sense objects, it is not external. Although...
It is not that the substance [of Buddha-nature] pervades both the internal and external; rather, because all sentient beings definitely possess this nature, it is said that "all have it.
Thus we know that Buddha-nature encompasses and includes all. How could it be restricted to the animate? Just as space is omnipresent, why would it be confined to the internal or external?

How could it be obstructed by walls, tiles, or rubble? Please observe the following two explanations of the scriptural meaning: since it is already stated that "space is in all places," [how could Buddha-nature be otherwise?]
Because it exists, one knows that the nature of the mind universally encompasses everything, even separating out tiles and rubble; for what could it not encompass?

Regarding the phrase "therefore we know," etc., it means that one does not permit the attachment that Buddha-nature exists solely within the six internal bases (*āyatana*), nor does one permit the attachment that Buddha-nature resides exclusively within the six external bases.
Thus, it says "neither internal nor external," which reveals that the essence of Buddha-nature pervades both the internal and external; hence, it is called "pervasive."
The phrase "it exists in all places" in the text includes the statement "neither internal nor external," as this serves to encompass the entire passage regarding its existence in all locations.
Furthermore, the thirty-second sutra also states: "I have taught that Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external so that sentient beings may attain understanding.
Why is this? Because ordinary beings may say that Buddha-nature dwells within the five aggregates, like [a substance] within a vessel."
Regarding that which exists within, some say it is separate from the aggregates (*skandha*) and exists like empty space; therefore, the Tathāgata has taught the Middle Way:
the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*) nor the six external sense bases, but because of their union, it is called the Middle Way.
Thus, it is proclaimed that Buddha-nature is itself the Middle Way. How could it be otherwise for the sutras to designate Buddha-nature as the Middle Way?

The state that is neither true nor conventional is called Buddha-nature. Therefore, because Buddha-nature as the Middle Way pervades all things, many sutras discuss its omnipresence in various places.
Since it is said to be "neither of the two," it must also be "both of the two. Thus, the sutra further states: "It is both internal and external.
If there were not this "bothness," how could one speak of its omnipresence? Consequently, [the text] refutes ordinary beings, or speaks of Buddha-nature [in this way].

If the Buddha-nature exists only within sentient beings—as the fruit within a vessel or as space, according to worldly parlance—then it is merely like the fruit in a vessel and cannot yet be reckoned as being like space;
how then could one understand it as being neither internal nor external?

Furthermore, the sutra itself explains that because the faculties and objects are joined, it is called the Middle Way. Since the faculties and objects are joined, are they not of one essence? Are they not of one characteristic?

If it is indeed the case that nature is all-pervasive, how can it be the same as the fruit of a vessel? Now I ask: is Buddha-nature a sense object (*viṣaya*), or is it a sense faculty (*indriya*), or is it both combined, or is it neither?
If it is neither, then it is not even the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

why then speak only of walls and so forth, or say it is "like space"? Since it is said that Buddha-nature is like empty space, and since empty space universally encompasses all things, it cannot be restricted to [a specific location].
Since it is stated that "internal and external" refers to the two lower realms, it is clear that this indicates their presence within the causes [of delusion].

Since it is stated that "sentient beings are in delusion," it is evident that the nature which is neither internal nor external, yet both internal and external, is simply the mind-nature of sentient beings pervading everywhere;
one must not become stuck on the words and fail to seek its reality.
Next, the second section clarifies the primary cause for the fruition of Buddhahood. Part one: citing the scriptural text. First, restating the meaning of the cause and posing a question.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa asks," this text appears in the thirty-third fascicle, prior to the section on the "Cause.
In the thirty-first fascicle, the Tathāgata used the analogy of empty space to illustrate the primary cause of Buddha-nature; therefore, Kāśyapa’s inquiry occurs within the thirty-third fascicle.

It is precisely for the purpose of inquiring into this meaning that the Sūtra states: The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said, “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space.
In what sense is it said to be ‘like empty space’? The Buddha then provides his answer through two Buddhas by way of the meaning of the fruit (*phala*).
Regarding the phrase “the unimpededness at the stage of fruition” and so forth: indeed, the Buddha’s response to Kāśyapa in the Sūtra consists of three sections.
Regarding the meaning of the fruition, it is first clarified that Buddha-nature is identical to empty space and is not encompassed by the three periods of time. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"Good son, because empty space is non-existent, it is not encompassed by the three periods of time; because Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not encompassed by the three periods of time.
Good son, the Tathāgata has already attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, and all his Buddha-nature and all Buddha-dharmas are eternal and unchanging. For this reason..."
Because of its meaning, the three periods of time do not exist, being like empty space. Next, it clarifies that, like empty space, it is neither internal nor external. The Sūtra says:
"Good son, because empty space is non-existent, it is neither internal nor external; because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is neither internal nor external.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature is like empty space. Third, it clarifies that, like empty space, it is without obstruction. The Sūtra says: "Good son..."

My son, just as that which is unobstructed within the world is called "empty space," so too, because the Tathāgata has attained *samyak-saṃbodhi* and is without any hindrance regarding all Buddha-dharmas, it is said that the Buddha-nature is like empty space.
For this reason, I say that the Buddha-nature is like empty space. In the present passage, the fact that it speaks only of being "unobstructed at the stage of fruition" is precisely [the point].
The intent of the subsequent section incorporates the previous two, because the scriptural passages of all three sections provide answers based on the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
Is it not the case that the latter two [sections] conclude with non-duality precisely because cause and fruit are mutually interfused and the three are without distinction?
When Kāśyapa asks about the *tathāgatagarbha* (the true cause of sentient beings), the Buddha answers in terms of the fruit; this is intended to reveal that cause and fruit are non-dual.

Regarding the second section, "Citing Scriptures from the Buddha’s Lower Two [Teachings] to Demonstrate that Expedient Conditions and Understanding are Difficult to Equal the True Cause," there are two parts. First, clarifying Kāśyapa’s objection. First, explaining the intent of the objection:

As for the answer given by the Buddha through the fruit of the ultimate teaching (*bhūta-śāsana*), it was because the Buddha responded to the analogy of emptiness using the unimpeded fruit-ground of the ultimate teaching.

Regarding "the fruit of the severance of expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna-prahāṇa-phala*): this refers to the cultivation of the understanding-cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) according to the expedient teaching, which results in the attainment of the fruit of wisdom through cultivation.

When the fruit of severance is accomplished through the conditions of *pratyaya* (enabling) and *jñāna* (insight), it is because the fruit of insight possesses the nature of realization (*parijñā*) and the fruit of severance possesses the nature of conditions (*pratyaya*).
Thus, these two fruits are said to possess both conditions and insight. Since both of these fruits involve both realization and vision, they are said to be "all existent.

As for the discrepancy between the dharma and the metaphor: the dharma refers to the existence of conditions and insight, while the metaphor refers to empty space, which is non-existent. This difference between existence and non-existence is vast.

This is not uniform; it is an objection based on the *pratyaya* (condition) and *hetu* (cause) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) to challenge the *zhengyin* (direct cause) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Specifically, Kāśyapa raises this objection because he considers that those with the faculties and conditions of the final age should hear the provisional teaching (*quanjiao*). Therefore, Kāśyapa subsequently cites two scriptural passages:

"Tathāgata" refers to the fruit of wisdom (*zhiguo*), and "Nirvāṇa" refers to the fruit of cessation (*duango*). The fruit of wisdom is the nature of *prativedha* (penetration/understanding). Cessation...
Since the fruit is of the nature of conditions, it is called Buddha-nature; one should know that the term "Buddha-nature" has no separate essence.

Therefore, while Buddha-nature occupies the central position, its meaning encompasses both the upper and lower [stages]. Although there are three names, they are merely the conditional and the innate; these are the two practices of the provisional teaching.
The Buddha first descends; the two Buddhas respond in two parts: first, the dual presentation of the two intentions.

Since Kāśyapa’s adherence to existence was for the sake of those with provisional capacities in the final age, the response follows his question. Nevertheless, because it extensively clarifies the pervasiveness of principle for those with ultimate capacities, it returns to the previous thesis to clarify that the metaphor of empty space differs from heterodox calculations.
First, following the question below; second, sequentially demonstrating the scriptural text. First, following the question.

The clarification of the existence [of nirvāṇa] has two parts. First, citing the scriptural text to show that it is taught as the principle of the quiescence of nirvāṇa in contrast to the non-quiescence of afflictions;
thus it says, "for those who are not," and so forth, with the other two cases being similar. Now, regarding the question below, there are two parts showing the meaning of the scripture.

First, restating the position and posing a counter-objection; this passage has two sentences: the first sentence restates the position, and the second sentence poses the counter-difficulty. The intent of the difficulty is as follows:
If one holds that tiles and stones are eternally devoid of Buddha-nature, then it would follow that those of the Two Vehicles and icchantikas would eternally lack the potential for Buddhahood,
and conditioned afflictions would never have an opportunity for cessation, because the scriptural passages state "non-existent" in all three cases.
If you admit that the essence of afflictions is itself nirvana and the nature of the Two Vehicles is itself the Tathāgata, how can you insist exclusively on the case of tiles and stones?
One must know that the statement "eternally non-Buddha-nature" is a provisional teaching; thus, one should understand that all such scriptural passages are expedient explanations.

Therefore, regarding the second section—the judgment and interpretation of the scripture’s intent—it is divided into two parts. First, clarifying the intent of manifesting the real while retaining the provisional: first, the formal judgment on retaining the provisional.

As for "relying on the provisional teachings of skillful means," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* primarily discusses the perfect reality of the true cause; now, in accordance with the suitability of the capacities of the audience, it temporarily [adopts a different approach].

Because the provisional teachings speak of the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the cause (*hetu*), it is said that they are "provisional" (*jì*). Regarding the three types of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*): to suppress afflictions is called "not *nirvāṇa*";
to suppress those of the two vehicles is called "not a *Tathāgata*"; and to suppress [the attachment to] tiles and stones is called "having no Buddha-nature.

These are all counteractive measures intended to urge sentient beings forward. The brief mention of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) is an explanation of the aforementioned "provisional" aspect of the skillful means (*upāya*) teaching.

The phrases respond to the occasion to briefly clarify the provisional (*upāya*), while the concluding text clarifies the ultimate meaning; therefore, it is said that "the teaching is temporary" because once afflictions are exhausted, there is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Apart from the two vehicles, there is the person of the Tathāgata, and Buddha-nature exists only within sentient beings;

since all of these are provisional teachings, it is said that "the three realms of existence" (*tridhātu*) serves to refute the three errors. This explains the aforementioned three antidotes. For now, let us rely upon...

The Sūtra speaks of "three" because there are three textual passages; in reality, however, there are only two natures, the conditioned (yuan) and the responsive (liao), as has already been explained above.
Furthermore, in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), it is not only the conditioned and responsive Buddha-natures that are separated from tiles and stones—the same applies to the true (zhengyin) nature.

Yet, Kāśyapa specifically uses the provisional fruit, the conditioned, and the responsive to challenge the real true cause. Therefore, the following two citations of the concluding text clarify this point.
Regarding the phrase "There is nothing that is not [empty]" at the beginning of the section on the two realities: "not" (fei) here means "no" (bu).

This means that among all things in the world, there is not a single entity that is not subsumed within empty space. Because empty space is beyond all relational opposition, it is said that "there is nothing that is not empty space"—meaning that even in contrast to empty space, there is nothing that is not it.
This serves as a metaphor for the principle of the three thousand dharmas as the true cause within the nature and mind of the Perfect Teaching.

Question: Since the inquiry throughout all sections accords with the provisional capacities of beings, and thus explains the provisional *pratyaya-bodhi* (conditional enlightenment) and *upāya-bodhi* (means-enlightenment), why does it nevertheless conclude by using the metaphor of the *tathatā-hetu* (true cause) of the Real Teaching?

Answer: The Tathāgata, wishing to protect those of provisional capacity in the final age who would otherwise find it unsuitable to hear that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, taught that the two vehicles are the Buddha-nature within the Tathāgata’s "tiles and pebbles.
Thus, he provisionally relied upon the teachings of the Expedient Means to explain the *pratyaya* and *upāya*.
Because there is suddenly a real capacity [in beings] that must not fail to be explained, the Buddha concludes by using the true teaching and the primary cause as metaphors.
Regarding the intention of the Buddha, the latter two parts explain the meaning of the sutra. The three items—tiles, stones, and so forth—are what are being contrasted;

that is to say, tiles and stones represent the afflictions of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), which are the objects of contrast, while Buddha-nature and Tathāgata-nirvāṇa are the subjects of contrast. When the former are contrasted with the provisional capacity, they are termed the "objects."
Regarding that which is not a counterpart, when contrasted with the actual capacity of the recipient, the entirety of the "object" is itself the "subject.

Thus, one knows that tiles and stones are themselves Buddha-nature, and that the Two Vehicles are themselves Tathāgatas, and that afflictions are themselves Nirvāṇa. Beyond these three—the Buddha-nature and so forth—there are no further distinctions such as tiles and stones.
Just as empty space has nothing with which it can be contrasted, it is said that there is nothing in all the worlds that is not emptiness.
Furthermore, one should know that emptiness and the others, as well as the Buddha-nature and so forth—these three are each three, yet each one is a fusion of the three;

they do not transcend the three thousand realms of one's own mind. These three thousand realms are the provisional nature, which is the *nidāna-hetu* (causal condition); this is *nirvāṇa*. These three thousand realms are the empty nature, which is the *vidyā-hetu* (revealing cause);
this is the *Tathāgata*. These three thousand realms are the middle nature, which is the *samyak-hetu* (correct cause); this is the *Buddha-nature*. How much more so in this case!
The three thousand realms, the three truths, the dependent and the primary, and the defiled and the pure encompass everything without exception;

how could there be bricks, stones, and so forth—these three—which exist solely outside the mind? Is the analogy of empty space not likewise so? Therefore, it is said that "all things are none other than the Tathāgata’s [threefold] nature.

Previously, in explaining the scriptural passage, the analogy of empty space was treated solely in terms of the non-duality of the causal and resultant aspects of the true cause (*zhengyin*); now, we explain the conclusion.

Question: Why does the text state that [the fruit] fully contains the three dharmas? Answer: Previously, it was explained from the perspective of their integration; integration fundamentally contains differentiation. Now, we discuss them according to their differentiation, yet this differentiation is not separate from integration.

Question: On the level of the fruit, is there only the nature of the true cause (zhengyin)? Answer: For now, we point to the three thousand realms manifested at the ultimate stage as the true cause on the level of the fruit.
In reality, the conditions (yuan) and the aids (liao) are one with the nature (xing); even at the stage of partial realization, this is already so.
How much less so in the ultimate sense?

Regarding the second section on "Kāśyapa’s Objections to Emptiness," there are two parts. First, Kāśyapa raises an objection based on a metaphor. This consists of three sub-sections. First, the indication:
[Kāśyapa] again takes the four great elements as a parallel, because the Buddha’s previous response concluded by stating that "there is nothing that is not empty space" in contrast to empty space.

He then sets forth a parallel argument, saying: "If the Tathāgata previously stated that space is non-existent because it is without counterpart, then the four great elements (mahābhūta) must also be non-existent because they too are without counterpart.
Conversely, if the four great elements exist despite being without counterpart, then space must also exist despite being without counterpart.

Thus, he says this so as to establish that space exists. Consequently, Kāśyapa, the two subsequent citations of scriptural passages show that there is nothing in the world that is not one of the four [great elements].
Regarding "the great elements" and so forth: it means that the nature of these four great elements pervades all places;

there is not a single location where the four great elements do not exist, such that they could serve as a counterpart to something else. This objection is raised based on the pervasiveness of the *nature* (dharmatā) of the four great elements, not based on their *characteristics* (lakṣaṇa).
Thus, if the nature of the four great elements can be said to exist because it is pervasive, why cannot the substance of space (ākāśa) also be said to exist because it is pervasive?

It is not called "existent," Kāśyapa; the following three passages demonstrate the intent of the sūtra. That which is great among existents is the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), for they have no counterpart.
Since space (*ākāśa*) also has no counterpart, it too can be called existent. Because this existence is without fault, it is said to be "great among existents.

Regarding the Buddha’s response below, he uses the analogy of the two Buddhas abandoning [the world] to answer in three parts: first, he cites the sūtra to illustrate that all three types are expedient abandonments through analogy.
Regarding the "follower of the Dharma," although Kāśyapa compared the four great elements to the Buddha, he ultimately did not provide an answer;

thus, it is said that he abandoned the analogy and merely cited empty space to correspond with *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is called "following the Dharma. Question: Why did he not answer? Answer: There is also a profound meaning here.
Kāśyapa originally stated that the four great elements have no counterpart, and for this reason they are called "existent. By extension, empty space should likewise have no counterpart.
Regarding this present clarity: although the four great elements (mahābhūta) do not exist externally as conceived by other schools, they do not arise from outside to confront the four great elements;

rather, within the four great elements themselves, there is mutual dependence, such that earth, water, and so forth each relate to one another. Furthermore, within empty space, there is no further entity that can relate to itself.
Therefore, these [conceptions] are non-existent, arising merely as empty fabrications; for this reason, the Buddha did not answer [the question], explaining it extensively.
Regarding the fact that *nirvāṇa* is not the same as empty space: *nirvāṇa* possesses fifteen meanings by which it differs from empty space, as stated in the Sūtra:
"Good son, if one says that *nirvāṇa* is subsumed within the three periods of time, and that empty space is likewise, this meaning is not so.
Why? Because (1) *nirvāṇa* exists; (2) it is visible; (3) it is realizable; (4) it is form; (5) it is a track; (6)..."
[It is] (7) a chapter-heading, (8) existence, (9) a characteristic, (10) a condition, (11) a refuge, (12) tranquility, (13) luminosity, (14) security, and (15) the further shore.
Therefore, it is designated as not being subsumed within the three periods of time. The nature of space does not possess such qualities;
therefore, it is called "non-existent. If there were any other phenomenon apart from these [qualities], [it would likewise be non-existent].
"If space were included within the three periods of time as a conditioned phenomenon (*dharma*), it could not be said not to be included within the three periods" (the above is from the sutra).
Thus, while there are fifteen propositions regarding *nirvāṇa*, there are no such fifteen propositions regarding space;
for this reason, it is extensively explained that *nirvāṇa* is not identical to space. This is why it says, "If *nirvāṇa* is not identical [to space]," and so forth.

Since the Sūtra extensively discusses how *nirvāṇa* and empty space are not of the same category, one knows by extension that *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) and the Tathāgata are likewise different from empty space.
Within the fifteen phrases concerning *nirvāṇa*, the meaning contains the remaining two [attributes], thus forming the three dharmas as all equally present;
this is forever distinct from the analogy of empty space. Is this not a teaching given by means of expedient devices? Therefore, it is known that what follows below proceeds toward [this conclusion].

The concluding passage represents the true meaning of the primary cause. Since the sutra text here states that nirvana and so forth are different from empty space, it follows that the nature of wisdom and severance in the provisional teaching differs from the meaning of the primary cause in the ultimate teaching.
Examining the preceding concluding passage, which states that "all worlds are none other than empty space," one understands that in contrast to empty space, the Tathāgata and others [are likewise].
The metaphor of being "equalized with empty space" is the conclusion drawn from the true cause according to the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).
Regarding the phrase "all worlds," how could the term "worlds" exceed the provisional designations of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the lands, and so forth?

Furthermore, since the colors of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*dhātu-āyatana*) pertain to both the Great and Small Vehicles, it is clear that not only the primary retribution (*vipāka*) is intended; thus we know this scriptural passage refers to "all worlds. The scripture says: "All worlds... [text continues].
There is nothing in between that is not empty space; for those who face this emptiness, the three realms of existence and so forth are none other than Buddha-nature.
The intent regarding the afflictions of the two vehicles can be understood from this. Since it is said that "all" is included, how could the afflictions and the two vehicles not be encompassed?
Thus, one knows that afflictions are themselves nirvana, and the two vehicles are themselves the Tathāgata. As for "empty space and so forth," empty space encompasses all that is vast.
If one realizes that tiles, stones, walls, and bricks cannot be discarded, then one knows that these tiles and stones are themselves Buddha-nature.
Thus, there is nothing in all the world that is not empty space; in relation to emptiness, they are fundamentally of one meaning.

However, to manifest that the essence of emptiness is all-pervasive—as previously explained—I have here used the term "all" to encompass the two vehicles and the term "emptiness" to include tiles and stones, employing these expressions in a reciprocal manner.

The literary style is such that when the question uses empty space as a metaphor for the bond, it reveals that the three—tiles, stones, and so forth—are themselves the three aspects of the Buddha-nature.

Is this not the fact that in the True Teaching (Shōkyō), the three causes are all universally pervasive? Why, then, does this passage speak only of the "direct cause" (shōin) in its formulation of the objection? Answer:

This is because it is intended to correspond to the provisional teachings (gonkyō) regarding the conditional and auxiliary causes; thus, for the sake of synthesis, it speaks only of the direct cause. Furthermore, since a synthesis must necessarily possess its opening counterpart, [the other two causes are implicitly included].
Because the three causes are all-pervasive, the thirteenth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Space is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and therefore it is eternal.
Space is precisely the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); the Buddha-nature is precisely the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is precisely the unconditioned; the unconditioned is precisely the eternal.
The sūtra further describes the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*), the Tathāgata as the revealing cause (*pariṇāmanā-hetu*), and the unconditioned as a synonym for nirvāṇa.
This very condition and cause is the sincere proof that the three natures are simultaneously one and three and universally pervasive.

"After the Buddha, descending again through three stages" indicates that the true cause of the Real Teaching differs from the provisional conditions and understanding. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha further says 'equal' and so forth," this refers to the extensive clarification that *Nirvāṇa* is not the same as empty space.
Since this passage follows the section concluding the difficulty regarding the True Cause (*zhengyin*), it is referred to as "after."
Furthermore, it is said: "Although the scriptural text is as cited above, the passages quoted therein merely capture the general outline and are supplemented with explanatory commentary;
therefore, they differ slightly from the actual scripture. Now, I shall cite the scripture and provide a word-for-word explanation so that the purport of the text may be seen.
Although emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and *nirvāṇa* are both not included within the worldly realm, the scripture states: 'Nirvāṇa is existent,' followed by fifteen [points]."
At the conclusion of the passage, it says: "Therefore, it is named as not being subsumed within the three periods of time. It further states:

"If empty space were the same as an existent dharma (*bhāva*), it could not be said not to be subsumed within the three periods of time. The present text, however, simply states that both space and *nirvāṇa* are not subsumed within the periods of time.
Regarding those who have realized and seen *nirvāṇa* and the Tathāgata, this refers to the fifteen aspects of *nirvāṇa* clarified in the Sūtra.
The phrase [in the text] states that "this exists" because it is visible and can be realized. Now, for the sake of further clarifying the meaning, the term "Tathāgata" is added;

this is because *nirvāṇa* is the fruit of cessation (*nirodha-phala*), whereas the Tathāgata is the fruit of wisdom (*jñāna-phala*). Since cessation must necessarily possess wisdom, the term "Tathāgata" is added by way of this implied meaning.
Regarding the statement that "space is eternal," the Sūtra says: "The nature of space does not have such phenomena; therefore, it is called 'non-existent'. Here, however, it is said to be "eternal."
Because that which is "constant" (nitya) is immediately devoid of meaning, Zhan’an said: "Emptiness is simply non-existence; non-existence is itself the constant. Therefore, it is not so.

As for the statement that "empty space is neither realized nor seen," the Sūtra says: "There is no such dharma. Is this not [the case]? In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Tathāgata has both realization and vision;
this refers to the provisional teaching where the conditions and causes (pratyaya-bhūta-hetu and upaniṣad-hetu) are empty space, and because it is constant, there is neither realization nor vision.

Because seeing is the true cause of the ultimate teaching, it is said to be "not the same. Thus, we know that in this section of the sūtra, the three causes are discussed through a comparative analysis of the provisional and the real:
when the provisional cultivation is contrasted with the real nature, the provisional cultivation is treated as two [factors], hence they are called the "conditions" (緣) and the "enabling" (了);

when the real nature is contrasted with cultivation, the real nature is treated as one, hence it is called the "true cause" (正因). This is the case if the provisional and the real are discussed separately.

Because the provisional cultivation (*prajñapti-bhāvanā*) consists of three [aspects], the preceding text states that the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature and *nirvāṇa* possess a real nature (*bhūta-svabhāva*), which likewise consists of three.
Furthermore, because the preceding text states that there is nothing in all the worlds that is not empty (*śūnya*), it is contrasted with emptiness.

However, according to the intended meaning of the sūtra, it correctly contrasts one portion [of reality] with the conditions of the faculties (*indriya-pratyaya*), and these two combined constitute the provisional cultivation as two. These two are not all-pervasive; they may be separated from insentient matter (*niścetanika*).

The true nature is one; since this One pervades all, how could it exclude even shards and stones? How much more so the True Teaching! Although they are integrated, this integration possesses distinct opening;

that is, the nature of the direct cause inherently possesses the conditions and the aids. When these natures are present, the cultivation is entirely perfected within the nature; when cultivation arises, the nature is entirely manifested through cultivation.
Thus, as the three aspects of nature pervade all, the three aspects of cultivation do likewise. Because the nature is pervasive, the Three Thousandfold World exists within the principle.
Therefore it is said: "Because the cultivation of the Buddha-nature of the insentient is pervasive, the perfection of the three thousand realms is itself the Buddhahood of the insentient;
cause and effect are non-dual, so how can the dependent and the primary be different? One must understand the three thousand realms to know that their essence is one.
One should not believe that the insentient possess the Buddha-nature while remaining skeptical that the insentient can achieve Buddhahood."
*The Record for Revealing the Nature through the Vajra Needle*, Scroll One;
*The Record for Revealing the Nature through the Vajra Needle*, Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān.

Next, following the Buddha’s descent [from the mountain], the text returns to its fundamental tenet to clarify emptiness. This section has three initial parts. First, it clarifies the intent behind returning to the fundamental tenet.

"Returning to the fundamental tenet" means that the Buddha originally used the analogy of empty space to illustrate the true positive cause (the *dharmakāya*). However, because Kāśyapa clung to the provisional aspects of the conditions and the understanding (*upāya* and *bodhi*) and challenged [the Buddha] by treating them as equally empty, the Buddha spoke of the three realms of existence to refute those three misconceptions.
He did so in accordance with the provisional teachings of the latter age to respond to his challenge, extensively discussing *nirvāṇa* rather than [merely focusing on] the three existences.
Having completed the exposition on its meaning as being identical to empty space, he returns once more to his original thesis to demonstrate that empty space is not a conditioned phenomenon;

thus it says, "to reveal that space is not existent. Furthermore, fearing that people of the world might take the space perceived by the eyes of non-Buddhists and worldly folk as a metaphor for Buddha-nature, he proceeds with ten further sections to provide a detailed demonstration, thereby preventing such erroneous interpretations. It should be said that there are ten [sections]; furthermore, they are called "ten."
First, regarding textual errors, the subsequent sections follow this same pattern.

At the beginning, it says "Below, two [sections]": first, citing the sūtra; second, the actual refutation of heterodox views. Within the first [section], there are ten parts. First, the refutation that emptiness is a mental factor (*caitta*). Within this, there are three parts:

first, citing the sūtra from "The people of the world" to "cannot be seen," which restates what is being clung to; then, following "The Buddha said," the refutation of this [position], namely that it is a mental concomitant (*caitta*).
This sutra states: "That which is formless, non-obstructive, and invisible is either a mental factor (*caitta*) or empty space.

If it were identical to a mental factor, it could not fail to be subsumed within the three periods of time. If it is subsumed within the three periods of time, it must consist of the four aggregates (*skandha*).
The present passage cites this only by capturing the general outline, or by altering the phrasing for the sake of easier understanding; the following nine sections are treated similarly.

For example, regarding the statement that resembles the second of the two explanations of the sutra—where it says the [nature of] speech resembles mental factors (*caitta*)—this does not mean that worldly people actually conceive of mental factors as being empty.

Rather, it is because the words used to describe empty space (*ākāśa*)—namely, "formless" (*arūpa*) and "non-obstructive" (*apratigha*)—are easily confused with mental factors, since mental factors are also formless and non-obstructive and cannot be seen.
It is for fear that people might take the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) to be analogous to such an empty space.
Because they hold such erroneous interpretations, the Buddha refutes them. Following the statement regarding the three periods of time, he concludes by likewise rejecting [their view].
The Buddha uses the analogy of space—which is eternal and abiding—to illustrate that the principle of *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) pervades all places;

yet, when worldly people claim that Buddha-nature does not pervade tiles and stones but exists only within the bodies of sentient beings, this is entirely identical to the non-Buddhist calculation that the mind-factors (*caitta*) constitute emptiness. This is because the mind-factors...

Because it exists within the body and because it is impermanent, those contemporary followers of the Mountain School who have not grasped the essential meaning claim that the contemplation of the inherent three thousand realms does not include the realm of phenomena; this view is likewise erroneous.
Second, refuting that emptiness is luminosity. First, the scripture is cited: herein, the opponent’s position is first restated, and then, from the words "The Buddha said," the refutation begins.

Since it is claimed that "emptiness is luminosity," one is reckoning empty space (*ākāśa*) as a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*). However, these non-Buddhists do not understand the meaning of emptiness;
they say that emptiness is color, yet this merely means that light and color are accommodated within emptiness. How can it be said, therefore, that emptiness itself is [the light]?
Is this form? Furthermore, the followers of the Sāṃkhya school also claim that the twenty-one forms include empty space as a form of luminosity.
Thus, one knows that if emptiness were form, it would belong to the impermanent and could not serve as an analogy for the Buddha-nature. Second, concluding by refuting the [opponent's] position:

if you claim that the Buddha-nature exists in sentient beings but does not exist in insentient things, how is this different from saying that light and color exist where there is illumination but do not exist where there is darkness?
It is simply non-existent.
Regarding the three refutations of emptiness as a dwelling place, the first cites a sutra which says: "Furthermore, there are those who say that empty space is a dwelling place.
Zhanran’s commentary explains: "As for 'dwelling place,' it means that empty space has a location, such as the east..."

In the second chamber to the west, one is full and one is empty; you should know that there is a location therein. Regarding this, the scripture cited merely quotes the opponent’s position while omitting the words of refutation, though these are fully contained within the sutra.
The sutra says: "If there were a dwelling place, it would be a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*);

yet all locations are impermanent and subsumed within the three periods of time. Space (*ākāśa*), however, is permanent and not subsumed within the three periods of time. If one speaks of a 'location'..."

Knowing that there is no such thing as empty space, both [theories] are equally rejected. It is not the worldly attachment that the Buddha-nature exists only within the bodies of sentient beings and does not pervade insentient things;
for this would confine the emptiness of the Buddha-nature to a specific location.
How is this any different from one room being full and the other empty?
The fourth [section] refutes the emptiness of sequence. This is the second [part of the section]. First, a scripture is cited, which says:

"Furthermore, there are those who say that empty space is itself sequential. Master Zhangan’s commentary on this states: "Regarding the term 'sequence,' it is like the interior of a flute or pipe, or like counting people as they enter through a doorway.
One sees the space outside within the window; first one sees it through the first lattice, and then again through the second..."
Regarding the second [point], within the third [section] one sees this sequence; here too, no refuting words are cited. The Sūtra says:

"If it were a sequence, it would be a numerical phenomenon (*saṃkhyā-dharma*); if it were numerable, it would be subsumed within the three times (*trikāla*). If it were subsumed within the three times, how could it be called eternal?
In both passages, no refuting words are cited because the locus of abiding is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*), whereas the sequence is a numerical phenomenon.

Since all these are impermanent and subsumed within the three periods of time, they are not metaphors for the Buddha-nature; this can be seen by analogy with the discussion on light, so there is no need for further elaboration.
Second, to conclude by equally refuting the worldly attachment that the Buddha-nature exists only within the bodies of sentient beings:

if this nature were located within the body, it would necessarily undergo change along with the body over time. If it were such a distinct entity, how would it differ from the calculation that regards space as [a material substance]?
This is incorrect in sequence.

Regarding the five refutations of space (*ākāśa*), they are contained within three sections; the first two initially cite a scripture, within which there is first a restatement of their position and then the refutation.

First, as for the restatement: they maintain that space has three aspects: (1) some say the "path of space" exists in the sphere of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*) and does not exist where there is no space; (2) others say space exists [in the sphere of space].

Regarding the passage on "existence" and "non-existence," it asks why there is no mention of "emptiness" among the three [categories]. It states that where there is existence and non-existence—such as a moist, decaying object—the state where it has not yet decayed is called "having emptiness.
The text says, "As for 'reality' (*satya*)," meaning that reality is precisely existence. The section beginning with "The Buddha said" below refutes the scripture;
every single phrase therein states, "One should know that empty space is an impermanent phenomenon. The first sentence of the scripture says, "If one says that space is..."

To know that empty space is an impermanent dharma: why? Because it is absent where there is substantiality. This passage consists of two phrases as an illustration; in the present text, some words have been omitted for brevity.
Furthermore, the character "is" (是) has been changed to "it" (者), and the character "substantial" (實) has been changed to "existence" (有), so that the text may be more easily understood.

As for "because it is absent where there is existence": since it is said that emptiness exists in the place of emptiness, one thereby knows that emptiness is absent in the place of existence, and that existence is absent in the place of emptiness.

Regarding that which is "without cause" (*ahetuka*): since it is said that emptiness exists within the state of existence, one knows that emptiness does not exist within the state of non-existence; because both states are absent. Regarding that which is "without cause":

since it is said that emptiness exists within the state of both existence and non-existence, one knows that emptiness exists within the state of emptiness and that emptiness does not exist within the state of existence.

This is like a decaying object: once its physical substance has perished, its momentum will not endure for long, and thus it is "also non-existent"; yet, because it is not yet utterly extinguished, it is "also existent."
If one maintains that space exists only where there are decaying objects, then it would follow that space does not exist where things are solid or where there is nothing at all.
Since space would thus not be pervasive, it would be impermanent and could not serve as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature.

Second, to conclude by refuting those worldly people who maintain that the Buddha-nature resides within the bodies of sentient beings: among their calculations regarding the three locations of space, they are merely clinging to a [limited] conception of space.
If emptiness exists only where there is something, then it is still deficient; for emptiness would lack existence both in places where there is emptiness and in places where there is nothing.
Such a view is inferior even to externalist doctrines—how could it possibly be the Buddha-nature?

Sixth, the refutation of the claim that emptiness is something produced has two parts: first, citing the sutra, which merely cites and restates [the opponent's position] without yet providing the refutation; within this restatement:

That statement is somewhat abbreviated, as the Sūtra says: "Some say that space is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), just as one speaks of 'removing trees' or 'removing a house' to create space;
one levels space, covers space, and exhausts the color of space within space, like the great ocean.
Therefore, space is a conditioned phenomenon. Now, when it says "removing a house" and so forth, the "and so forth" (*ādi*) [indicates further examples].
Taking away trees or even painting [the image of] empty space—this refers to the calculation of outsiders who maintain that emptiness is not obtained through natural causes or creative action.
Just as when one cuts down trees or dismantles a house, this place becomes empty, they thus know that empty space is obtained through the act of creation;

therefore, it is said that emptiness is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). As for what is said in the Sūtra regarding "level covering" and so forth, these are easily understood. As for "painting empty space" and the like, these are merely [the views of] outsiders.

If you claim that human testimony proves space can be created—meaning you assert that the color of space can be depicted in a painting, its form vast and spreading like the appearance of the ocean’s waters—then since the color of space can be so depicted, it must be verified as a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). In the Sūtras, the Buddha himself refutes this, saying:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, just like a clay jar. If space were such [a thing], it would necessarily be impermanent.
The second point, "criticizing both [views] equally for being non-identical to the body’s dissolution and so forth," means:

if one were to claim that only upon the destruction of the body does one correspond with the true principle of *nirvāṇa*, then how would this differ from the void that exists only after leaving a house? Therefore, the Sāṃkhya and other schools all maintain that digging the earth or cutting down trees results in the attainment of emptiness;
these are all instances of "producing emptiness" (*kṛtaka-śūnyatā*), which are equally false conceptions. This [passage] is based on this [point] to constitute the criticism.
The attachments held by the teachers of the Hīnayāna are equally erroneous and have no bearing on the Mahāyāna conception of Buddha-nature;
perhaps they belong elsewhere, but their specific intent remains unclear.
Seventh, the refutation of emptiness as being unimpeded. Part two: first, citing a sūtra; therein, first the restatement [of the opponent's position], then the refutation. First, the restatement:
That is to say, space has non-obstruction as its nature, such as apertures and cavities, which are termed "space. A sutra states:
"People of the world say that among all phenomena, that which is without obstruction is called space. The Buddha said [this] to refute it. Herein, the cited text is obscure;
the sutra first establishes [the definition] with two lines, then raises an objection to what was previously established. The sutra says: "This state of non-obstruction, in all..."

Regarding the phrase "that which is fully possessed" (*yǒufēn yǒujù*), the current text states: "there is the portion that possesses" (*yǒufēn yǒujù*). The Buddha first established the intent [of the question]:

if one asks whether the unobstructed place is empty, is this emptiness fully capable of containing the emptiness of the ten directions, or is it not fully capable of containing the emptiness of the ten directions?
Next, he challenges [the opponent] by citing the Sūtra: "If it were fully possessed, one should know that there would be a remainder."
If space were non-existent in its location, yet could be divided into parts, it would be a phenomenon that can be counted as "this" or "that.
If it were countable, it would be distinct and known to be impermanent. Now, when the text says, "because it is absent in other locations," this merely cites one side of the argument.
Furthermore, the text appears to be incomplete; following the phrase "if it were fully present," one should add: "because it is absent in other locations. This is the intended meaning of the passage.
Regarding the Buddha’s intention in posing this difficult question: if the ten directions were filled with empty space, one should know that there would be no empty space in the ten directions;
if they were not joined together, it would mean that what exists here is absent there.

Second, the conclusion equally refutes those who, like worldly people, cling to the notion that *ākāśa* (space) and *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) exist within sentient bodies but do not exist in insentient things—this is entirely identical to the externalist calculation of spatial apertures (*chidra*).

Within the center, the ten directions are encompassed by emptiness; if this were reversed, the ten directions would consequently lack emptiness. Therefore, it is said that "in other places, there is none.
Eighth, the refutation of both emptiness and existence. This section has two parts: first, citing the sutra, where the scripture is initially quoted as follows:

"If someone says that emptiness is unobstructed and exists in conjunction with existence," the Buddha says: [The following is] next, the refutation within the sutra, which first establishes three topical headings. Second, ...
Now, to explain the three categories of conjunction (*saṃyoga*): the Sūtra states that if one speaks of conjunctions, there are three kinds:
first, conjunction through distinct karma (*visabhāga-karma*), such as birds gathering in a tree; second, conjunction through common karma (*sabhāga-karma*), such as two rams butting heads;

third, conjunction through already-conjoined common karma, such as two pairs of fingers joined together in one place. Zhiyi (Zhang’an) explains: "First, conjunction through distinct karma is like birds gathering [in a tree]."
As for "tree," it is simply that birds come to perch upon the tree; the tree does not go to perch upon the birds. It is also like this:
when things come together with emptiness, emptiness does not go to combine with things. When these two—emptiness and things—combine, they are like leaves meeting, or like two rams butting heads.

Emptiness combines with things, and things also combine with emptiness. Third, their combined union is like the joining of two pairs of fingers; the function of the things has already combined with the things themselves.
This is the essence-function; this is the function of things. These two matters—essence and function—are already united with emptiness, and emptiness is already united with them.

Emptiness is the essence and function is emptiness; that which is contained is by means of this essence-function already united, and is further united with things, like two fingers that have already joined and then join together again. This is explained in sequence in the Sūtra.

The third chapter explains the scriptural text of the first chapter by raising three difficulties: the difficulty of impermanence, the difficulty of permanence, and the difficulty of both permanence and impermanence.
Regarding the difficulty of impermanence, the Sūtra says: "If one says that different karmas combine together, then there are two [entities]:

first, the karma of material objects, and second, the karma of space. If the karma of space combines with material objects, then space would be impermanent; if the karma of material objects [combines...]"
If empty space were not pervasive, it would likewise be impermanent. Zhan’an’s commentary explains: "First, the activity of matter is the activity of movement;
second, the activity of empty space is the activity of emptiness. Regarding the statement that if the activity of emptiness conjoins with matter, then emptiness is impermanent:
since matter is already impermanent, how could emptiness—which conjoins with it—not also be impermanent? If it conjoins with the activity of matter...
"If that which is empty does not pervade, then since this [the object] is conjoined with that [emptiness], it should likewise pervade according to emptiness;

furthermore, the object should follow emptiness and thus be eternal. Since the object does not pervade, how can it be conjoined with emptiness? If the object is impermanent, would emptiness also be impermanent?
The sūtra further raises the objection regarding permanence and the objection regarding both permanence and impermanence (etc.). This concludes the commentary on the second chapter.
The Sūtra says: "If it were combined with collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*), this meaning would not be correct.
Why? Space is called 'pervasive' (*vyāpin*); if it were combined with karma, then karma too should be pervasive. If it were pervasive, it should be pervasive of all things;

if it were pervasive of all things, it should be combined with all things. One should not say there is combination and non-combination. Zhiyi’s commentary explains: "If space were combined with karma..."
"Furthermore, that which is pervasive should also [be pervasive]" means that since the essence of emptiness and its function are conjoined, the function should likewise be pervasive.

If the function of emptiness is pervasive, it should then be pervasive in its conjunction with things; there can be no emptiness apart from things. One should not speak of there being both conjunction and non-conjunction.
Regarding the explanation of the third chapter, the Sūtra says: "If one says they have already conjoined, it is like two fingers joined together. This is the meaning.

Otherwise, for what reason? Because there was no prior conjunction and only later did conjunction occur; because it was non-existent before and existent after, it is an impermanent phenomenon (*anityadharma*).

Therefore, one cannot say that space has already conjoined or conjoins together with [other things]. Just as worldly phenomena are non-existent before and existent after, such objects are impermanent.
If space were like this, it too would necessarily be impermanent. Zhiyan’s commentary states: "As for the phrase 'non-existent before'..."

Regarding "subsequent existence," this refers to the case where emptiness and a thing were not conjoined at a prior time but are only conjoined at a subsequent time; thus, what was originally non-existent now exists, and it should therefore be impermanent. However, this [argument] only refutes subsequent conjunction and does not refute prior conjunction. The reason for this is that the essence of emptiness and the functional activity of emptiness, as well as the essence of a thing and the functional activity of a thing, must either both be non-existent or both be existent. If they are non-existent, they are already so; if they are existent, they are both so. Thus, there can be no such thing as one being existent while the other is non-existent. Therefore, the principle of "original non-existence and present existence" does not apply here. Consequently, the meaning of "subsequent existence" is untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the essence of emptiness and the essence of a thing are distinct," this is also incorrect. Why? Because if the essence of emptiness and the essence of a thing are distinct, then when the essence of emptiness is empty, the essence of the thing should also be empty; and when the essence of the thing is existent, the essence of emptiness should also be existent.
