As for disciples of dull faculties who seek much and engage in discrimination—even those with superior resolve—Śrīmati addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You should know that those of joyful faculties are deceptive and delusive."
When those people fell into wrong views and declared that sensual desire is an unobstructed dharma, at that time Nandimukha thought to himself:
"These people are shrouded by the karma of great hatred and evil; they shall fall into great calamity. I should now preach the profound Dharma for them to serve as a cause for future lives.
He immediately assembled the community of monks and at once spoke this verse: "Sensual desire is itself the Way."

The same applies to hatred and delusion; through these and more than seventy other verses, thirty thousand devaputras attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and eight thousand śrāvakas all attained liberation.
At that moment, Śreṇika’s body immediately fell into hell, where he suffered for thousands of myriads of years.
When he was reborn among humans, he was constantly slandered for seven hundred and forty thousand lifetimes, and for immeasurable kalpas he did not hear [the Dharma].
The names of the Buddhas caused his offenses to gradually diminish, so that he was able to hear the Buddha-dharma, leave the household life to practice the Way, and yet again abandon the precepts.

Thus, for sixty-two thousand lifetimes, he constantly abandoned the precepts. Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, although he acted as a śramaṇa and did not abandon the precepts, his faculties were dull and dark.
However, Xi-gen (Joy-root) has now become a Buddha in the eastern direction; his buddha-land is named Bao-yen (Jewel Adornment), and his name is Guang (Light).
Beyond the passing of days and months, at that time, the one named Superior Intention was none other than my own self.

You should know that both "Not Disparaging" and "Joyful Faculties" were all powerful [beings] who proclaimed the complete and sudden Dharma; they truly did not delight in acting as distant causes for others.

Although they initially slandered the Dharma and fell into suffering, they ultimately attained liberation. It is like placing poison in food: while the true cause of the mind-nature is likened to the food, hearing [the Dharma] is like the poison.
The *liǎoyīn* (revealing cause) dharma is like administering poison; later, when the poison manifests, death is certain beyond doubt.
Thus it is said that the "strong poison" (*qiángdú*) of the *Shòuléngyán* refers to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva.

I now cite this sūtra to prove the matter of the "strong poison" of Nandika’s joy and the falling into hell for slandering the Dharma, which is like falling while already on the ground due to one's own causes. Furthermore, it is due to... [text truncated]
The fruit-seeds will attain liberation in the future, arising as they did on the causal ground.

This section consists of two parts: first, the instruction on how to apply great compassion; second, the formal demonstration of the method for circulation. Regarding the first, "one should apply great compassion," etc., it means:

one should give rise to great compassion and pity for those who have not yet awakened, and in accordance with their habitual practices, point out that the mind is inherently complete. If this is done for the sake of surpassing others...

To use the "perfect" (round) teaching to reprimand those who are "partial" is called "distressing others. Why? Because if one does not yet know the recipient's capacity (*indriya*), and that person originally lacks the great capacity, yet one forcibly applies the perfect teaching, it will conflict with their disposition and cause distress.
Furthermore, if the partial practitioner is reprimanded while the perfect practitioner remains unresolved regarding their prior doubts, they may later regret;

thus, both the partial and the perfect are lost. Is this not distressing others? However, if one is in a state of sainthood (*ārya*), one skillfully discerns the conditions of the recipient and knows that through such subduing...

Only those who have benefited may censure or admonish others, yet even when observing whether they are progressing or regressing, if they possess faith and comply with the teaching, one should point out their inherent potential.
If they resent the teaching and engage in contention, one should instead apply the "Dharma of Not Disparaging. Thus it is said that one should observe whether they are progressing or regressing;

to follow what they are accustomed to is called "protecting their minds," which is why the *Anrakugyō* (Practice of Peace and Bliss) states: "One should not delight in speaking of persons or scriptures."
How much more so regarding the "Peaceful Practices," which correctly demonstrate the method for the transmission of the teaching in the final age;
by showing that the mind is inherently complete, one accords with the original intention, for this was the fundamental purpose of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.

If there are those of the lower two capacities, [the text] correctly demonstrates the methods and procedures in two parts. First, regarding the application of the methods shown in the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices) for those who seek benefit by following the teachings in accordance with them, there are four sections.
First, directly demonstrating the Great Dharma for those who have not yet received the provisional teachings.

Within this, first, directly demonstrating the wondrous principle of Buddha-nature. Within this, first, revealing the three meanings. Within this, first, showing that the seed-nature is entirely the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Third. [End of section].

As for the causes: afflictions are the nature of the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*), karmic bonds are the nature of the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), and the path of suffering is the nature of the true cause (*tattva-hetu*).

These are understood through their mutual opposition when viewed from the perspective of their actual entities, corresponding to such dualities as phenomenon and principle, cause and effect, delusion and awakening, and bondage and liberation.

From beginning to end, the principle is one, and the meaning of waves upon water may be inferred by analogy. Furthermore, it should be known that the three paths within the hundred realms are all identical [to the ultimate reality].

The three causes and the three natures are mutually fused and inseparable within a single thought-moment; yet, for now, the hundred realms are presented as belonging to the essence and its qualities, merely to indicate the seed-nature so that one may know it exists.
Regarding the "unmanifested" and so forth: "arousing the mind" refers to hearing the name and recognizing the essence, thereby giving rise to perfect faith;

"preparatory application" refers to adding correct cultivation and auxiliary practices, thereby establishing perfect conduct. This is because [the practitioner] has not yet aroused the mind [of aspiration].

Therefore, there is no cultivated virtuous *niṣyanda-hetu* (causal condition) because there has never been any preparatory application (*prayoga*); and there is no cultivated virtuous *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause) because [the text] omits "ever" in the preceding phrase and omits "from" in the following phrase—this is due to the nature of the text.

As for the phrase "because it has not yet arisen" (*ayata*), this is an error; it should be read as "because it has come from" (*āyata*). Regarding the term "identical with the direct cause" (*samyag-hetu*):

although sentient beings have possessed the three natures since beginningless time, because they remain in delusion, these are established as names based on the principle (*tattva*); thus, they are the principle.

Because the middle three [stages] are all subsumed under delusion, they are combined with the nature (dhātu) into one; thus, they are collectively termed the "three types of the true cause" (*saddhātu-jāti*).

Furthermore, because *nirvāṇa* is also spoken of in terms of this combination, it is called the "true nature" (*saddhātu*). Question: At what stage do the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) occur? Answer:

They occur within the stage of names (*nāmadheya-bhūmi*), wherein the ten vehicles of practice (*daśayāna-pratipatti*) are established based on the understanding of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun-jie*). If...

Question: For what reason did you previously state that the three types of wisdom are combined into one at the stage of names and letters (*nāma-pada*) as the "revealing cause" (*paridīpana-hetu*)? Answer:

At the stage of names and letters, once the mind has been aroused and preparatory practice (*prayoga*) undertaken, one truly possesses both the objective condition (*ālambana*) and the revealing cause. However, in relation to the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) upon entering the five grades (*pañca-varga*), at this stage of names and letters one possesses only the revealing cause;

thus it is termed "receiving" (the revealing cause). It is only upon reaching the five grades and the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) that one separately attains the designation of the "objective condition. This is a matter of inclusion and exclusion based on the specific context.

Although this is so, in reality, both the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the causes (*hetu*) exist at every stage. For instance, when the five grades [of practitioners] and the six faculties all employ the ten vehicles, these very ten vehicles encompass both the cultivated (*bhāvanā*) and the inherent (*prakṛti*).
Here, the inherent seeds and correct practice constitute the cause, while the auxiliary practices that open [the way] constitute the condition.

Thus, that which is illuminated by the conditions and the causes is precisely the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*). This is the threefold turning of the rational nature (*li-xing*), which becomes the objects, wisdom, and practices of cultivation.
The three "excellent" [factors] derive their names from this very principle of being received through intensity; they are collectively bound as three, yet practiced individually as one or two.

Regarding the nature (*prakṛti*), it is as previously explained in terms of stages. Therefore, various texts explain them according to practice, stating that the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the cause (*hetu*) each have three aspects;

or they discuss the rational nature (*li-xing*), which possesses all three from beginning to end, as in the passages concerning the "three paths," the "three virtues," and the "three Buddha-natures. Furthermore, regarding the conditions and the cause in this school...

The gradations of rank and the principles of inclusion and exclusion are not limited to a single path. According to the *Commentary on the "Life Span" Chapter of the Lotus Sutra*, all stages prior to the first abiding (*prathamā bhūmi*) are collectively considered the "causal condition" (*nidāna-hetu*);

it is only upon the true realization of the first abiding that one is designated as the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*), because even a Śrāvaka who hears the sutra and receives a prediction of enlightenment immediately enters the first abiding.
However, according to the *Commentary on the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs"* chapter, the stage of ultimate perfection is termed "wisdom," while the intermediate stages are termed "understanding."

The fourth [point] is that all are subsumed within the three aspects of practice (*pratipatti*), because they accord with the scriptural text which culminates in the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

Thus, at the beginning of the "Excellence of Practice" (*xing-miao*) in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), the "Identity-in-principle" (*li-ji*) is taken as the threefold nature (*svabhāva*); the "Names-and-words" (*ming-zi*) are taken as the threefold wisdom (*jñāna*);

and the "Contemplative Practice" (*guan-xing*) and "Similarity" (*xiang-si*) are taken as the threefold practice (*pratipatti*), because the excellence of these three dharmas is manifested in the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). Therefore, the conditions (*pratyaya*) and causes (*hetu*) are both [included].

Because they exist prior to abiding, the *Fenbie Gongde Pin* (Chapter on Distinguishing Merit) says: "The object is inherently endowed with the three; because one generates understanding based on principle, it is called wisdom," and so forth.

Therefore, what is discussed by this school does not go beyond these various meanings. If one were to specifically indicate the cultivation and nature for a beginner, one must rely on the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning);

its meaning is precisely the same as that of the present text. Furthermore, the names "cultivation" (*xiu*) and "nature" (*xing*) apply generally to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), and within the Separate Teaching...
Although there are statements regarding cultivation and nature (*xing*), if all three [aspects] reside solely in nature without being mutually integrated, they constitute a distinct meaning;

if all three reside in cultivation and are attained sequentially, the principle constitutes a serial (vertical) relationship. One should know that in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), whether in terms of nature or cultivation, all three are perfectly wondrous.
This relationship between cultivation and nature is the vital core of our school; because later students are largely confused by it, I have exerted diligent effort here.

Question: Since *diligence*, *questioning*, *cessation* (*śamatha*), *contemplation* (*vipaśyanā*), the "ten dharmas that form the vehicle" (*daśa-dharma-yāna-sampad*), and "patience" (*kṣānti*) pertain only to the five stages [of the ten faiths], and "separation from craving" pertains only to the six sense faculties, why does it say that one cultivates the "ten vehicles" (*daśa-yāna*) at the stage of "name and word" (*nāma-pada*) and so forth? Answer: There is both a general and a specific sense.

In the general sense, the ten dharmas are cultivated in every stage; this is as stated in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), which says that within the single true stage (*eka-bhūta-avasthā*), one begins by cultivating them starting from the stage of "name and word."
In practicing the ten vehicles to enter the first stage and even up to the stage of partial realization of truth, one must employ the ten types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*);
because these are taught separately to correspond to the three faculties [of sentient beings], they are mutually elucidated throughout both the general and specific categories.

Having already established faith, the following two sections demonstrate the essence and the magnitude [of the mind]. First, the seed-nature is demonstrated, like pointing to a single wave as being water;

next, the essence and magnitude are demonstrated, like showing that water pervades the hundred rivers. "Internally" refers to the six sense faculties, and "externally" refers to the six sense objects.

Because the essence of the mind-nature pervades both the internal and external, it is not restricted solely to either the internal or the external. Therefore, it is not merely that it pervades the internal and external; it pervades all of empty space. Although empty space is vast, the mind...

Because the nature is also universally identical to the essence of all Buddhas, it is said to be "the same as all Buddhas. Because it is equal to the nature of sentient beings, it is said to be "equal to the dharma-realm.
Thus, the *Fenbie ermen* (Treatise on the Non-duality Gate) states: "The dharmadhātu of the Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings are without distinction;
the substance of their nature is entirely pervasive."

Having already established faith in the preceding section, this section below demonstrates the essence and virtues [of the nature]. First, the direct demonstration of the essence and virtues: the eternal possession of the three thousand [realms] within the nature.

Once one has realized that these are inherent virtues, one must know that the nature, which is fundamentally pervasive, eternally possesses the three thousand realms; the environment and its inhabitants are interfused, being no different from those of a Buddha.
This is like realizing that water pervades all rivers—one must know that at the location of a single wave, the nature of all river-waves is inherently present.
Thus we know that those who discuss the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and point to True Suchness (tathatā) do not intend [merely] this;
for while all Buddhas have already perfected [this state], sentient beings merely possess the Buddhas' capacity for mutual fusion.

Because sentient beings possess the principle of mutual fusion, the fruit is cited as perfected to demonstrate the inherent nature (prakṛti). Since the measure of the defiled body and the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) are equal, one body is precisely one [with all].
Because the realms of the sensory dusts (*viṣaya*) are no different from the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*), one land is all lands;

this is the non-duality of the three bodies (*trikāya*). Regarding the mutual identity of the four lands and the single body-land: the preceding two phrases still discuss the fusion of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*) individually;
furthermore, one must understand that the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, such that the four lands are the three bodies and the three bodies are the four lands.
Because the three lands and four teachings are mutually integrated and not separate from the nature of the mind, when the body speaks, it is called the land speaking;

yet the lecturer merely says that the *kṣetra* (land) speaks and sentient beings speak, without considering who it is that acts as the speaker and the recipient among both the *kṣetra* and sentient beings.

This is truly due to a failure to contemplate the nature of sentient beings and the *kṣetra*. If one grasps this meaning, then all things are mutually illuminated, and the Great and Small Vehicles become one.
"Many" refers to two among the eight masteries (*vaśitā*). The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 21, states: "First, regarding 'one and many': [the Tathāgata] manifests a single body as many bodies;
the number and size of these bodies are like motes of dust, filling the ten directions. Yet the body of the Tathāgata is not actually dust;
it is through mastery that he manifests bodies like motes of dust. Second, regarding 'small and large': he manifests a single mote-of-dust body so that it fills [the world]."

Third, regarding lightness and heaviness: though his body fills the great trichiliocosm, he can lift it lightly and fly through the air; yet in reality, there is neither lightness nor heaviness. Fourth, as for the form-body and mind:
the Tathāgata dwells with single-minded composure and immovability, yet he manifests and transforms himself into immeasurable forms and types.
Fifth, regarding the faculties: the six sense-faculties function interchangeably. Sixth, regarding attainment: he attains the mind of the Tathāgata regarding all dharmas. Furthermore—
Seventh, even if one were to preach and expound a single verse for immeasurable eons, its meaning would never be exhausted.
Eighth, the body of the Tathāgata pervades all places; like space, it cannot be apprehended or seen. In this text, the first two points are briefly cited to encompass the latter six.
Although sentient beings lack the eight kinds of sovereign power (*vaśitā*), they possess the nature of sovereignty.

For example, because the land is embodied, it is said that "it is likewise so. That all Buddhas attain this great function is precisely due to the principle of the three thousand realms being manifested;
since the principle of the three thousand realms is inherently possessed by sentient beings and is equal to that of the Buddhas, it is said that they possess the nature (buddha-nature).

Regarding the first of the three sections of the first layer of the initial [part], which refutes both the two lower schools of this world and the tenets of other traditions by establishing only the pure nature:
it merely asserts that the self-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is intrinsically pure and, through following conditions, can manifest as either defilement or purity;

yet it fails to realize that the pure nature of True Suchness inherently possesses the three thousandfold realms of both the defiled and the pure, including the environment and its inhabitants. This is just as if one were to merely assert—
The moisture of water can manifest as clear or turbid waves, yet the moisture of water does not realize that it inherently possesses the nature of clear and turbid waves.

As for the phrase "adding those myriad practices," the character "those" (彼) is likely an error and should be "cultivating" (修); this refers to the functional essence [of practice], as others have said:
"The dharma-body of True Suchness is empty and pure by nature, but because it is defiled by the stains of ignorance and afflictions, it must be maintained."

The various cultivations of precepts, concentration, and wisdom result in pure function only upon reaching the fruit; this is precisely the essence of the myriad practices within the cause serving as the functional utility within the fruit.
This is what is discussed by the contemporary religious schools and is commonly known to scholars.

Regarding the refutation of the lower two [positions]: since the Buddha-fruit is nothing other than the originally pure nature, if it possesses function, it conversely becomes the existence of a Buddha.
Since the great function of the fruit-nature is accomplished through cultivation, sentient beings who are lost in delusion possess only the pure nature.

If this pure nature does not yet possess the great function, how can one say that these sentient beings have Buddha-nature? Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* proclaims with utmost emphasis that birth possesses Buddha-nature;
how can you establish a doctrine that specifically contradicts that sūtra? Thus, it is known that if one understands the present school’s [view on] birth...

The Buddha’s three thousand worlds are from beginning to end a single, unified whole. Since all Buddhas possess the principle of mutual fusion, sentient beings likewise possess the principle of mutual fusion;

thus, the teaching that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is clear and self-evident. Having understood that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, one also knows that Buddhas possess the nature of sentient beings.
Because sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, when they encounter favorable conditions, they can skillfully manifest and realize the realm of Buddhahood.
Because sentient beings possess the nature of Buddhahood (*gotra*), they are struck by the stimulus [of the Buddha's compassion] and give rise to the response of the nine realms.

Others clarify that those who have severed all roots of goodness (*icchantika*) are permeated by the *ālayavijñāna*; yet they can still give rise to goodness, for the *ālaya* is itself indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) ignorance, serving as the support for both good and evil and acting as the storehouse for all seeds. This is because *icchantikas* do not sever this indeterminate ignorance.
When one returns to birth as a virtuous Buddha, the indeterminate ignorance has been severed and exhausted; since there is nothing further to be perfumed, evil no longer arises.
If one wishes to transform sentient beings through evil, one merely employs supernatural manifestations to deliver them. This requires deliberate intent (*manasikāra*) to give rise to evil;
it is not a spontaneous transformation and is entirely a matter of conceptual thought. How does this differ from the heterodox *abhijñās*?
Your argument that transformation occurs without deliberation turns into mere sophistry; the analogy of a mirror reflecting images is therefore of no use.

It is evident that you have not heard the name "inherently evil nature" (xing-è) and are entirely ignorant of the principle of "inherently good nature" (xing-shàn). You must understand that because the Buddha-fruit possesses inherently evil nature, it is called "not severed" (bù-duàn);
because it possesses cultivated evil nature, it is called "not eternal" (bù-cháng). If both the inherent and the cultivated were exhausted, then...

All things are such that they cannot be severed; thus they are neither interrupted nor eternal. Consequently, the nature of an icchantika’s goodness is not severed and can still give rise to wholesome roots;
likewise, the nature of a Tathāgata’s evil is not severed and can still give rise to evil. Although evil arises, it is the mind of liberation;
therefore, while the Tathāgata understands [evil] yet is not defiled by it, the icchantika is defiled yet does not understand it. This is the distinction between them. (1)

I request that you, as a student of the household, take the principles of cultivating nature and the meaning of good and evil, along with the statements regarding neither permanence nor discontinuity, and distinguish them one by one;
through diligent discernment, you will have already grasped more than half the meaning of cause-and-principle and effect-and-function. The aim of "discontinuity within continuity" lies therein.

The three lower sections provide three exhortations. Since the *Avataṃsaka* has already shown that the mind creates all phenomena, it now concludes by identifying the relationship between sentient beings and Buddhas.
If all are thus, is it not because each rational nature (li-xing) individually creates the three thousand realms, such that these mutually pervade one another?

Only then can they be called "without difference," which accords with the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the existence of the Buddha-nature (*gotra*). If one were to claim that sentient beings possess only a pure nature while the fruit of Buddhahood is achieved through cultivation as a great function, then distinctions would remain vividly apparent;
where, then, would the principle of "each creating" reside? This is the verification and the proof. Now, it is said that both sentient beings and Buddhas [are identical].
The presence of the "Three Thousand Worlds" serves as the scriptural evidence for the non-differentiation [of phenomena]; I address this to those who engage in exegesis:
do not turn your backs on this sutra by asserting merely that there is a pure nature (*śubha-svabhāva*). Question:

Since the *Avataṃsaka* states that the mind creates all varieties of things, is it not the case that the originally existent pure nature can, in accordance with conditions, perform such creative acts? Why then must one insistently establish that the nature itself is replete [with all phenomena]?

Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), [the questioner] asks: "If their nature (*svabhāva*) were not inherently complete, how could they be produced? One should know that the capacity for production arises entirely from the inherent completeness of nature.

For example, water can produce waves only because water inherently possesses the nature of waves. It is for this reason that the doctrine established by our school is eternally distinct from all other schools;

that we personally heard it from the Buddha on Vulture Peak is precisely due to this. Thus, one knows that although what is discussed by other schools may reach a state of profound interfusion and identity..."

Since it does not discuss the meaning of perfect fusion, its significance remains unclear; if compared to our present school, it is neither Perfect nor Distinct, nor is it the Tripitaka or Shared [teachings], though it may be so characterized by way of contrast.
Nevertheless, when discussed in comparison, it can be said to possess a partial sense of the Perfect.

If one says that the second section of the lower part [of the treatise] first narrates how this arises from the preceding objection and then addresses the opponent’s counter-argument, it is because they say:

"If it is claimed that there is a pure nature prior [to fruition] which becomes functional upon reaching the fruit, this both contradicts the teaching that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and runs counter to the scriptural passage on the non-differentiation of the three [natures]. Therefore, they further argue: "When it is said that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature..."

This is because the original, inherent, correct cause—the pure nature (*viśuddha-dhātu*)—of sentient beings is equal in principle to the *dharmakāya* of the resultant Buddha; thus it is said that "sentient beings possess the nature.
Since the correct cause is equal to the *dharmakāya*, the meaning of the three being without distinction is established.

However, because they are not equal to the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, it is said that one must apply effort in practicing the myriad practices so that, upon reaching the fruit, there is great function. This is the "great function."

This refers to the Retribution and Transformation bodies. To say that these still constitute the lower two [bodies] and are thus "sentient beings" means that because the Retribution and Transformation bodies possess great functional utility, the solitary Dharma-body is no different from sentient beings.

Even if the Dharma-body possesses the "correct cause" and so forth, although it avoids the fault of having the nature of a Buddha's birth, it still incurs the error of having the nature of a sentient being's birth; therefore, it is not yet [fully realized as] beyond being a sentient being.
There is the meaning of the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, regarding the third section of the second part of the lower three [sections], the initial exposition states that the so-called Dharma-body is not something solitary;
rather, it is equal to the great functioning of the *saṃbhoga*- and *nirmāṇa*-bodies. Because of this, there is established the meaning that sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature. Its...

As stated below, since it is already admitted that the *dharmakāya* possesses the functions of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, one knows that the *dharmakāya* is not separate from the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.
Because the locus of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* is entirely the *dharmakāya*, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* says:
"Śākyamuni is named Vairocana. Based on this, the nature of sentient beings fully possesses the three bodies of the resultant Buddha; therefore, [it is] impossible [to deny this].

It is said that while the pure nature alone does not possess the three thousand [realms], one must realize that the nature inherently possesses the three thousand; thus, when the fruit is attained, there is great utility.
The three thousand as the provisional (prajñapti) are the nature of the *nirmāṇakāya*; the three thousand as the empty are the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*;
and the three thousand as the middle are the nature of the *dharmakāya*. Because the sentient beings' minds inherently possess the three thousand, they are the nature of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
It is said that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

Now, these two [subsequent] sections below serve as a conclusion to demonstrate the three names. Previously, it was stated that from beginningless time there have been only afflictions, karma, and suffering;

therefore, it is said that "demonstrating existence" means that these very things are entirely the rational nature (*li-xing*) of the three causes. Thus, it is said that this demonstrates the "seed-nature" (*zhong-xing*), which is none other than the three paths (*san-dao*).

These are called "lineage" (*gotra*) because they are the seeds of the three natures; because they possess the nature of arising, they are termed "seeds. At the time of their arising, these seeds transform purely into cultivation (*bhāvanā*); since the nature of cultivation is one and possesses no separate essence, and because its principle remains identical from beginning to end, it is termed "nature" (*prakṛti*). Is it not true that waves are the seed-nature of water, and water is the wave-nature? Furthermore, there are two further distinctions regarding the meaning of "seed": 1. The seed as the cause of arising. 2. The seed as the cause of transformation. The first refers to the seeds of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which are the causes for the arising of the various phenomena of the three realms. The second refers to the seeds of the transforming consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which are the causes for the transformation of those very phenomena. These are the two meanings of "seed. As for the term "nature," there are likewise two meanings: first, the nature of the seeds themselves; second, the nature of the phenomena produced by those seeds. Because the seeds are the basis for the arising of all phenomena, they are called "nature. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds are the basis for the cultivation of the path, they are also called "nature. Thus, the seeds are the nature of the phenomena, and the phenomena are the nature of the seeds. This is why it is said that the nature of the seeds is the nature of the phenomena, and the nature of the phenomena is the nature of the seeds. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "cause": first, the nature of the cause itself; second, the nature of the fruit. Because the seeds are the cause for the arising of the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of the cause. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds are the cause for the cultivation of the path, they are called the "nature of the fruit. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "cause. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "result": first, the nature of the result itself; second, the nature of the cause. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds are the result of the seeds, they are called the "nature of the result. Because the seeds are the cause for the production of those phenomena, they are called the "nature of the cause. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "result. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "function": first, the nature of the function itself; second, the nature of the agent. Because the seeds produce the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of the function. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds cultivate the path, they are called the "nature of the agent. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "function. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "substance": first, the nature of the substance itself; second, the nature of the attribute. Because the seeds are the substance of the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of the substance. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds are the attributes of the seeds, they are called the "nature of the attribute. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "substance. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "pervasion": first, the nature of pervasion itself; second, the nature of what is pervaded. Because the seeds pervade the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of pervasion. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds pervade the seeds, they are called the "nature of what is pervaded. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "pervasion. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "inclusion": first, the nature of inclusion itself; second, the nature of what is included. Because the seeds include the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of inclusion. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds include the seeds, they are called the "nature of what is included. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "inclusion. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "support": first, the nature of the support itself; second, the nature of the supported. Because the seeds are the support for the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of the support. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds are the support for the seeds, they are called the "nature of the supported. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "support. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "transformation": first, the nature of transformation itself; second, the nature of the transformed. Because the seeds transform into the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of transformation. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds transform into the seeds, they are called the "nature of the transformed. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "transformation. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "manifestation": first, the nature of manifestation itself; second, the nature of the manifested. Because the seeds manifest the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of manifestation. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds manifest the seeds, they are called the "nature of the manifested. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "manifestation. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "arising": first, the nature of arising itself; second, the nature of what arises. Because the seeds give rise to the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of arising. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds arise from the seeds, they are called the "nature of what arises. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "arising. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "cessation": first, the nature of cessation itself; second, the nature of what ceases. Because the seeds cease along with the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of cessation. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds cease along with the seeds, they are called the "nature of what ceases. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "cessation. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "emptiness": first, the nature of emptiness itself; second, the nature of what is empty. Because the seeds are empty of the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of emptiness. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds are empty of the seeds, they are called the "nature of what is empty. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "emptiness. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "existence": first, the nature of existence itself; second, the nature of what exists. Because the seeds exist as the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of existence. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds exist as the seeds, they are called the "nature of what exists. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "existence. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "non-existence": first, the nature of non-existence itself; second, the nature of what does not exist. Because the seeds do not exist as the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of non-existence. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds do not exist as the seeds, they are called the "nature of what does not exist. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "non-existence. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "permanence": first, the nature of permanence itself; second, the nature of what is permanent. Because the seeds are permanent as the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of permanence. Because the phenomena produced by the seeds are permanent as the seeds, they are called the "nature of what is permanent. This is the meaning of the two aspects of "nature" within the sense of "permanence. Furthermore, there are two meanings of "nature" within the sense of "impermanence": first, the nature of impermanence itself; second, the nature of what is impermanent. Because the seeds are impermanent as the phenomena of the three realms, they are called the "nature of impermanence.
